    # Frontmatter
    
    # Preface
    
    In many scientific fields, including polymer science and nanotechnology, artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming research approaches. This interdisciplinary collaboration promises faster discovery, material design, a better knowledge of structure-property correlations, and greater customization and innovation potential. This book explores the role of AI in polymer design and characterization. The chapters discuss a wide range of subjects, including autonomous self-driving labs for material innovation and AI-enhanced polymeric drug delivery systems. To address difficult design problems, forecast polymer properties, enhance material performance, and uncover underlying relationships between structure and functioning, the book additionally discusses the use of machine learning in materials science.
    
    The aims of the book are: to inspire future research at the intersection of data science, material informatics, nanotechnology, and polymer engineering; to introduce readers the basic and emerging applications of AI in polymer and nanomaterial research; to outline the technologies, methodologies, and frameworks reshaping material discovery; and to demonstrate the role of AI to develop autonomous, predictive, and scalable research models.
    
    The book is aimed at a wide range of readers, including research scientists, graduate and postgraduate students, academic scholars, industry engineers, and technology developers, who are interested in the exciting convergence of AI and materials science. It provides useful perspectives and practical insights for academics and industrial experts.
    
    # Foreword
    
    The potential of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning has triggered a revolutionary shift in the fields of materials science and polymer technology. AI has accelerated innovation by identifying hidden patterns, forecasting the characteristics of materials, creating molecular structures, and automating entire labs. This book is a significant scientific contribution in the field of polymer science. The book, edited by Dr. Rishabha Malviya and his team, provides an in-depth discussion of the role of AI technologies in nanoscience and polymer technology. The chapters in this book demonstrate a careful balance between theoretical frameworks, state-of-the-art research, and practical applications.
    
    Since polymeric materials are essential to consumer technology, biomedical applications, environmental sustainability, and drug delivery, the book focuses on the applications and societal aspects of these developments. AI integration enables faster, smarter, safer, and more sustainable solutions that prioritize society and the environment.
    
    The book invites researchers, engineers, academics, and students to adopt a new paradigm of data-driven, autonomous, and intelligent material discovery. It is not simply an academic book but a blueprint for the future. Through his efforts and leadership in bringing together an excellent group of contributors, Dr. Rishabha Malviya has compiled a book that will be an essential resource for present and future scholars working at the convergence of AI, polymer science, and nanotechnology.
    
    Happy reading and best wishes,

    # Chapter 1 Nanotechnology innovation: AI\-enhanced polymer drug delivery systems
    
    Wan Nurhidayah Khan Aejaz Ahmed Usama Ahmad 
    
    #### Abstract
    
    The confluence of polymer nanotechnology with artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing drug development and targeted drug delivery, ensuring unprecedented precision in therapeutics. By coupling data analytics with AI\-driven polymeric nanocarrier systems, the technology surpasses the constraints of traditional drug delivery, including bioavailability and patient-specificity, by virtue of superior design, encapsulation efficiency, and controlled release mechanisms for the drug. Predictive modeling and machine learning algorithms aid AI in optimizing drug–polymer interaction and optimizing the physicochemical characteristics of polymer nanocarriers so that therapeutics are released accurately and controllably at target sites to reduce side effects. AI’s capability to forecast the interaction of disease-specific, biocompatible, and responsive polymers for patient profiles advances the principle of precision medicine. Improved encapsulation efficiency and optimized kinetics by AI\-driven processes maximize the direct delivery of therapeutics to the target site with optimal doses for enhanced bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. The amalgamation of AI with polymeric nanotechnology thus enables drug discovery in the rapid prototype and optimization of nanocarrier systems to deliver precise, individualized drug delivery with high accuracy to diverse therapeutic domains. This chapter discusses the development potential of AI\-fortified polymer-based drug delivery systems, their ability to maximize the efficacy and selectivity of treatment regimens. With AI\-driven innovation, polymer nanotechnology has the ability to improve patient treatment through highly personalized and potent medical options, beginning a new era of tailored medicine and new paths of drug innovation.
    
    Keywords:  Artificial intelligence,  targeted drug delivery,  polymeric nanocarriers,  nanotechnology,  precision medicine,  machine learning,  personalized treatment,  
    
    ## 1.1 Introduction to AI and polymeric nanotechnology in drug delivery
    
    Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming contemporary drug delivery systems by increasing formulation and optimization of therapeutic systems. AI finds the most appropriate drug delivery systems tailored to patients’ specific requirements, improving treatment efficacy \[[1](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_001)\]. In pharmaceutical technology, AI\-driven models predict drug–polymer interaction, improving stability, controlled release, and efficiency of the drug carrier \[[2](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_002)\]. Machine learning allows quick innovation, with the ability to design nanoparticles with desirable characteristics, optimizing targeted drug delivery with reduced development time and expense \[[3](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_003)\]. AI optimizes bioavailability by forecasting drug behavior in the biological system, resulting in improved absorption and therapeutic action \[[4](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_004)\]. AI utilizes patient-specific data to enable treatment individualization on the basis of genetic profiles to optimize clinical gain \[[5](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_005)\]. This technological advancement redrew pharmaceutical sciences, offering smart and efficient drug delivery strategies. Design and development of targeted drug delivery systems are presented in [Figure 1.1](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_fig_001), with AI integration.
    
    ![Figure 1.1: Design and optimization of targeted drug delivery system with integration of AI.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-001_fig_001.jpg)
    
    Figure 1.1: Design and optimization of targeted drug delivery system with integration of AI.
    
    The combination of AI and polymer nanotechnology has revolutionized materiomics, biomedicine, and drug delivery by improving the design, optimization, and functionalization of polymeric nanocarriers. Machine learning and deep learning in AI speed up the identification of polymer membranes for use in carbon capture and cancer therapy by predicting polymer composition, drug uptake, and controlled release, streamlining timelines and accuracy \[[6](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_006)\]. Polymeric nanosystems such as nanoparticles and vesicles have shown greater stability, tunability, and capacity to entrap more than one therapeutic agent, which is useful for addressing complicated diseases such as triple-negative breast cancer and resistant cancers \[[7](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_007), [8](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_008), [9](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_009)\]. AI has facilitated the development of polymeric systems that can be designed to emulate biological cells, allowing cellular behavior to be accessed with ease and drug delivery to be optimized \[[10](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_010)\]. Advanced models have maximized functionalization of nanostructured lipid carriers to enhance cellular recognition, which is crucial for targeting diseases such as chronic inflammation and chemotherapy-resistant cancers \[[11](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_011)\].
    
    AI algorithms predict the self-organization and spatial arrangement of polymer-modified nanoparticles, which maximize the controlled release of drugs and cell targeting \[[12](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_012)\]. Emerging trends involve the combination of MXenes and polymers in nanocomposites for drug delivery and diagnostics, where AI maximizes design and therapeutic effectiveness \[[13](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_013)\]. AI\-aided polymer nanoparticles have been synthesized via processes like double emulsion and pH-triggered synthesis, which enhance bioavailability and treat bacterial infections \[[14](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_014)\]. AI\-aided polymeric systems are being studied in neuromorphic computing, where polymer devices exhibit synaptic behavior for brain-inspired computational modeling \[[15](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_015), [16](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_016)\]. These advancements show the way AI\-polymer nanocarriers offer possibilities for precision medicine, targeted therapy, and other biomedical progress.
    
    ## 1.2 Design and optimization of targeted drug delivery systems
    
    ### 1.2.1 Accurate prediction of molecular interactions
    
    Latest advances in computational algorithms enhanced predictive capability to engage in interactions with higher precision and effectiveness when higher accuracy and efficacy are needed. Some models, such as the SPVec-SGCN-CPI model, use a simplification of graph convolutional networks to predict compound–protein interactions using neighborhood information and topological features, outperforming other approaches in imbalanced data \[[17](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_017)\]. The SSGraphCPI model utilizes a three-channel deep learning model, integrating sequential and structural features of 1D SMILES strings and 2D molecular graphs, showing outstanding performance in datasets such as GPCR \[[18](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_018)\]. The LINE network representation approach utilizes a heterogeneous multi-molecular information platform to predict interactions with high precision \[[19](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_019)\]. Integration of molecular and interactome information through sophisticated deep learning architectures enhances the accuracy of prediction by integrating views beyond sequence homology and structural similarity \[[20](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_020)\]. Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) have been developed to simulate molecular dynamics with ab initio accuracy, solving issues such as nonlocal interatomic interactions \[[21](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_021)\]. Approaches to predicting binding free energies through end-state molecular dynamics simulations have shown strong correlation with actual data, which offers a lower-cost alternative to classical approaches \[[22](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_022)\]. Advances such as AlphaFold2 for protein–protein interaction prediction \[[23](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_023)\] and the CREST tool for exploring conformational spaces in receptor–ligand binding \[[24](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_024)\] enhance the accuracy of molecular interaction prediction and hence improve drug discovery and advance the knowledge of biological processes.
    
    ### 1.2.2 Optimization of polymer properties
    
    Polymer property optimization involves an integrated method that includes advanced computational methods to maximize polymer performance and application. Multimodal deep-learning models are a forefront method that combines physical and chemical data to forecast properties of advanced polymer composites across extensive compositional ranges. The method facilitates handling of high-dimensional data in inverse material design with optimized properties \[[25](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_025)\]. Transfer learning of injection molding processes has been employed to optimize machine parameters based on limited data, demonstrating AI capability to enhance process efficiency and product quality in polymer processing \[[26](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_026)\]. Quantum computing facilitates optimization of polymer attributes by sampling dense polymer mixtures at equilibrium using quantum annealing technology, allowing polymers with designed structural properties \[[27](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_027)\]. AI application in designing multifunctional composites of MXene and graphene blends displays innovation in advanced multifunctional composites, indicating AI capability in designing materials with improved thermal, electrical, and mechanical properties for smart electronics \[[28](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_028)\]. In silico methodologies, such as molecular mechanics-driven multi-monomer concurrent docking, facilitate the optimization of molecularly imprinted polymers through the assessment of monomer combinations to enhance binding capacities, thereby improving the sensitivity and selectivity of artificial receptors \[[29](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_029)\]. Such methods greatly facilitate optimization of polymer properties, enabling advanced material design with improved performance and functionality.
    
    ### 1.2.3 Development of predictive models for biocompatibility
    
    Synthesis of polymeric biocompatibility predictive models requires understanding the interactions between biological systems and polymeric substrates. Recent research has revealed key determinants of biocompatibility, which have assisted predictive modeling. Microporous scaffolds by stereolithography cellular compatibility is improved by postprocessing methods, including ultraviolet irradiation and Soxhlet extraction, eliminating residual toxic monomers \[[30](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_030)\]. Similarly, swelling behavior and crosslinking density in ionic liquid-containing hydrogels affect biocompatibility, with evidence from cell seeding experiments using L929 mouse fibroblasts \[[31](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_031)\]. Polysaccharides, naturally occurring and biodegradable, are of interest in drug delivery due to low immune reactivity and efficient release kinetics \[[32](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_032)\]. Copolymers containing thioester functionality, degrading amid physiological thiols, are of considerable significance in the realm of pharmaceutical delivery, owing to noncytotoxic breakdown products \[[33](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_033)\]. Electron beam-irradiated carboxymethyl chitosan hydrogels in wound healing display excellent biocompatibility in vitro and in vivo \[[34](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_034)\]. Addition of natural biopolymers, including starch and gelatin, in composite membranes improves compatibility with biological tissues, as evidenced by in vivo implantation studies \[[35](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_035)\]. Bioinspired polymeric materials that replicate cell membranes demonstrate enhanced biocompatibility in biomedical devices \[[36](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_036)\]. Hydrophilic polyphosphoesters show minimal interaction with blood components, demonstrating the contribution of polymeric chemistry to hemocompatibility \[[37](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_037)\]. Parameters such as polymeric architecture, crosslinking density, degradation behavior, and postprocessing techniques are indicated by these findings as determinants of significant influence on biocompatibility. These variables, when included with predictive models, improve the design of safer and more efficient biomedical materials while reducing extensive biological tests.
    
    ### 1.2.4 High-throughput screening
    
    The technique of high-throughput screening (HTS) of polymers poses high importance, mostly in industries ranging from materials science and pharmaceuticals to environmental science, with emphasis on rapid identification and evaluation of polymer properties and potential applications. HTS has screened biopolymers such as chitosan and cationized cellulose nanofibrils to be screen printed on polypropylene substrates for facial masks, enhancing antiviral activity, while retaining viral filtration efficiency \[[38](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_038)\]. HTS accelerates automation of simulations for new material discovery, such as using the many-body perturbation theory to surpass density functional theory limitations for increased-level simulation convergence in materials science computations \[[39](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_039)\]. Screening through HTS for antimicrobial agents, accelerating the discovery of small molecules stimulating antimicrobial peptide synthesis, offers a platform for new therapies \[[40](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_040)\]. HTS screens single-particle acidity of the catalyst, giving insight into activity and compatibility with fluid catalytic cracking processes \[[41](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_041)\]. HTS is also leading in drug discovery, which is evident through the identification of small molecule inhibitors of proteins from pathogens like *P. falciparum*, which is critical to the development of antimalarial therapy \[[42](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_042)\]. Utilization of HTS in such applications speaks volumes about its usefulness and significance in speeding up compound discovery and optimization across a variety of scientific disciplines.
    
    ## 1.3 Enhancing encapsulation and controlled release
    
    ### 1.3.1 Enhancing encapsulation
    
    The encapsulation within a suitable polymer involves diverse factors, which includes chemical structure of the polymer, molecular weight, and functional groups, influencing encapsulation efficiency and stability of the encapsulated compound. For instance, in encapsulation of cold-pressed hickory oil, β-cyclodextrin (β-CD) and porous starch (PS) possessed great encapsulation efficiencies of 80.40% and 75.52%, respectively, compared to maltodextrin and hydroxylpropyl-β-cyclodextrin, owing to conformational stability of the structure and heat stability, which are critical for oil oxidative stability maintenance \[[43](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_043)\]. The replacement of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) with linear polyglycerol (LPG), in the presence of Interferon-α2a, strongly regulates the pharmacokinetics and efficacy of bioconjugates, with PEGylated variants showing increased levels of exposure \[[44](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_044)\]. The physicochemical properties of poly-vinyl polymers, such as vinyl pyrrolidone-to-vinyl acetate ratio, regulate the efficiency of amorphous solid dispersions, modulating the dissolution and solid form stability \[[45](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_045)\]. The balance of cationic-hydrophobic functionality is important in the optimization of antibacterial efficacy and selectivity and reflects how the application of specific functional groups optimizes encapsulation efficiency through enhanced interaction with target molecules \[[46](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_046)\]. Entrapment of hydrophilic agents in extracellular vesicles demonstrates the significance of encapsulation procedures, where freeze-thaw and osmotic shock procedures are capable of achieving high drug encapsulation while preserving vesicle properties \[[47](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_047)\]. These examples demonstrate that the choice of a polymer is a complex process requiring careful consideration of the purpose of application, stability requirements, and interaction dynamics with the encapsulated entity to introduce increases in efficiency and performance.
    
    Machine learning models and AI\-based simulations maximize nanoformulation processes through optimization of comprehension and regulation of the properties of polymers. Machine learning models forecast the gas-separation behavior of polymers, illustrated by Barnett et al., who forecasted performance of over 11,000 homopolymers from a small dataset, developing membranes beyond the state-of-the-art performance for CO[2]/CH[4] separation \[[48](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_048)\]. AI\-based digital twins, as illustrated by Davidopoulou and Ouranidis, offer realistic in silico simulation of the manufacturing process, enabling optimization of nanosuspension formulations by forecasting and controlling the output from experimental data \[[49](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_049)\]. The combination of machine learning and infrared thermography facilitates automatic forecasting of the properties of polymer composites, required for the optimization of formulation \[[50](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_050)\]. Transfer learning, as illustrated by Tsubaki and Mizoguchi, facilitates forecasting of polymer properties by utilizing pre-trained models with small molecules, gaining insight into quantum-chemical properties of polymers \[[51](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_051)\]. Utilizing machine learning models, combined with Bayesian optimization, as illustrated by Lampe et al., facilitates rapid optimization of nanocrystal syntheses, providing potential to enhance material homogeneity and quality with limited data requirements \[[52](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_052)\].
    
    ### 1.3.2 Controlled release profiles
    
    Mathematical modeling of release kinetics of controlled release of polymers utilizes different models to maximize drug delivery systems. Polysaccharides, owing to their biocompatibility and biodegradability, are widely used in nanoscale synthesis to encapsulate drugs and release, where mathematical models predict matrix behavior, minimizing experimental trial and error \[[53](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_053)\]. For chitosan/alginate membranes, kinetic models such as zero-order, first-order, Higuchi, Korsmeyer–Peppas, and Weibull functions examine release profiles, where the Weibull model fits some forms of membranes optimally \[[54](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_054)\]. Chitosan particulate carriers illustrate the pivotal role played by mathematical models in describing particle structure and release kinetics relationship \[[55](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_055)\]. Coupling physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models with release kinetics permits simulation of systemic exposure over an extended period of time and release parameter optimization \[[56](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_056)\]. Design of experiments (DOE) and physiologically based biopharmaceutics modeling (PBBM) in extended-release formulation development predict absorption and formulate design optimization \[[57](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_057)\]. Programmable self-regulated molecular buffers provide an innovative strategy for maintaining target drug concentrations \[[58](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_058)\]. Coordination between drug release and targeting, as illustrated with lipid-like polymer nanoparticles, underlines the critical need to balance release behavior with targeting capability \[[59](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_059)\].
    
    Stimuli-responsive polymer systems have opened new doors for achieving accurate and efficient drug delivery. These systems are triggered by internal and external stimuli, which widely probe to maximize the aimed therapeutic effect and controlled drug release. In gene therapy, stimulus-sensitive nanocarriers release therapeutic nucleic acids, triggered by responding to physiological conditions such as pH changes and redox gradients, within tumor microenvironments \[[60](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_060)\]. Nanomedicine platforms with distinctive properties allow for more effective drug delivery in cancer treatment through a response to microenvironmental stimuli such as enzyme activity and pH levels \[[61](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_061), [62](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_062)\]. The mechanism of drug release is increased with integration to AI by evaluating biological conditions and predicting the best release patterns. Through modulation based on patient-specific data, AI models are able to maximize drug delivery to obtain better accuracy and outcomes. Smart hydrogels and nanomaterials that respond to biological and environmental stimuli are investigated for their potential uses such as antimicrobial coatings and demand-driven drug delivery \[[63](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_063), [64](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_064)\]. Such systems have the potential to deliver therapeutic drugs that are triggered by particular stimuli, reducing systemic side effects and optimizing the therapeutic outcomes \[[65](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_065), [66](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_066)\]. AI is also able to facilitate on-time monitoring and adaptive drug release control, which allows for personalization of the treatment regimens. Hence, the prompt-responsive material synergy of AI is setting the stage for innovative healthcare remedies with higher specificity, lower side effects, and greater adaptability to patient demands \[[67](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_067), [68](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_068)\]. Integration represents a revolutionary new approach in controlled drug delivery, with a new line of more intelligent, efficient therapeutic regimens. Machine learning algorithms can improve accuracy in real-time monitoring systems of regulated polymer release by analyzing complex data and forecasting system behavior. Integration of machine learning with spectroscopic methods, i.e., deep ultraviolet Raman spectroscopy, allows accurate identification and quantification of chemical pollutants in environmental monitoring, which can be applied to polymer release monitoring by discriminating specific spectral features of polymer release or degradation processes \[[69](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_069)\]. Machine learning models, particularly with deep neural networks, can adjust parameters of coarse-grained models of polymers, enhancing the accuracy of predictions about polymer behavior under different conditions such as temperature fluctuation and stress relaxation \[[70](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_070)\]. Application of recurrent neural networks in predictive control structure modeling can improve real-time control of complex systems by forecasting control-relevant parameters, crucial for maintenance of target release rate in polymer systems \[[71](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_071)\]. Advanced feedforward neural networks, with optimization methods, have improved prediction accuracy for complex systems, such as wastewater treatment, by identifying nonlinear relationships and avoiding overfitting, which can be applied to polymer release monitoring \[[72](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_072)\]. Convolutional neural networks have been promising in analyzing high-dimensional data, such as fluorescence spectra, to forecast chemical by-products, which can be applied to monitoring specific release of polymer constituents \[[73](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_073)\]. Real-time monitoring systems for regulated polymer release are challenging, mainly due to limitations, primarily because of complexities in accurate forecasting and regulation of release profiles in dynamic environments. One such vital limitation is compatibility between pharmaceutical agents and carrier materials, restricting the loading capacity and overall efficiency of drug delivery systems. This is countered with sophisticated techniques, such as the sequential solidification technique, which improve drug loading and release control by encapsulating drug nanoparticles in a polymeric matrix, as shown by high drug-loaded microspheres for spinal cord injury therapeutic use \[[74](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_074)\]. Dynamic characteristics of polymer interactions in systems that fluctuate pose a consistent challenge to standard monitoring methods, which tend to require static geometries of the sample. AI\-based spectroscopic methods offer a desirable strategy by enabling rapid, real-time evaluation of structural alterations, with no limitations posed by standard strategies \[[75](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_075)\]. The capacity of AI in handling large amounts of data as well as in identifying low-dimensional patterns within complicated systems can be utilized to enhance flow control in polymer release systems so that there can be more adaptive and accurate regulation mechanisms \[[71](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_071)\]. AI also helps in enabling the development of feedback-controlled adaptive biomaterials, e.g., hydrogels that release anti-inflammatory drugs, upon activation by certain biological stimuli, to enhance the safety and efficacy of polymer-based drug delivery systems \[[76](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_076)\].
    
    Polymeric systems of controlled release and AI hold immense potential in sustaining the stability and longevity, which is truly evident by a number of empirical analyses. Polylactic/glycolic acid (PLGA) has been utilized to prepare microspheres for payload delivery in single, time-delayed doses in a controlled fashion to provide patient compliance and therapeutic efficacies \[[77](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_077)\]. Hence, involvement of AI can optimize release profiles by anticipating and responding to release kinetics with real-time inputs, which can render therapy more effectively. Sustained drug release and mathematical modeling facilitate the prediction of release dynamics, which can be optimized through AI software to reduce trial and error by experimentation \[[32](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_032)\]. The potential of AI can be utilized for nanofibers that facilitate photothermally controlled release to regulate external stimuli, such as light, to release drugs at the most appropriate time intervals \[[78](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_078)\]. Supramolecular micelles for antioxidant encapsulation, such as fullerene, illustrate the potential of AI to manipulate environmental factors such as temperature to regulate the release mechanism \[[79](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_079)\]. Drug delivery to tumor site has been enabled by polymeric micelles and with the presence of AI, the process can be further improved by fine-tuning stimuli-responsive processes to release drugs \[[80](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_080)\]. Encapsulation of bacteriophages in PLGA/alginate composites to enhance in vivo viability illustrates the ability of AI to monitor and control release to maintain therapeutic concentrations for long periods of time \[[81](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_081)\]. Inflammation-reactive hydrogels for drug release, in response to particular biological triggers, can be designed with AI, which could identify inflammation and modulate release \[[76](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_076)\]. Merging polymer blends and AI in controlled release is a promising area of research for maximizing medical use of drug delivery systems in aspects of stability, durability, and efficacy.
    
    ## 1.4 Personalized and disease-specific treatment approaches
    
    ### 1.4.1 Customizing nanocarriers for patient profiles
    
    Individualization of nanocarriers from individualized genetic and molecular profiles of patients requires a list of vital factors, as discussed by various applications and methodologies in relevant scholarly literature. First, employment of microRNAs (miRNAs), encapsulated in nanocarriers, against cancer stemness, for example, melanoma, necessitates the choice of miRNAs possessing the ability to modulate epigenetic signaling cascades. This necessitates nanocarriers to provide maximum entrapment efficiency, stability, and specificity to allow the delivery of such miRNAs, and potentially with chemotherapeutic drugs, to enhance therapeutic effects \[[82](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_082)\]. Moreover, mechanical properties of nanocarriers, e.g., silica nanocapsules, can be designed to govern the delivery of encapsulated drugs, in response to external mechanical stimulation, which is essential to targeted drug delivery and release to the target site \[[83](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_083)\]. In ocular diseases, lipid-DNA nanoparticles demonstrate the importance of nanocarriers to possess better biodistribution and sustained release, offsetting such limitations as rapid diffusion of drugs and poor tissue retention \[[84](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_084)\]. Lastly, the development of stimuli-responsive nanocarriers for gene therapy, responsive to physiological or external stimuli, demonstrates the critical importance of smart delivery systems able to target the therapeutic agents to the target site and overcome biological barriers \[[60](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_060)\].
    
    Personalization of nanocarriers to the individual patient profiles in their biological and metabolic environments requires advanced technologies and complete awareness of the individual needs of each patient. Three-dimensional printing technologies, investigated in personalized medicine, allow the fabrication of customized nanomedicines to conform to the individual physiological profiles of patients, such as metabolic rates and biological milieus \[[85](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_085)\]. Personalization is of critical significance in illnesses such as ulcerative colitis, where sensitive nanosystems can direct pharmacological agents to the area of inflammation, producing maximum therapeutic responses and minimum systemic side effects \[[86](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_086)\]. Nanocarrier modulation of the innate immune response can be optimized to modulate infection and inflammatory processes in patients with varied immune profiles \[[87](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_087)\]. In the treatment of chronic wound healing, nanocarriers may be formulated to disassemble biofilms and release therapeutic molecules at wound sites, considering the patient’s microbial niche and immune system \[[88](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_088)\]. Control-programmable molecular buffers that regulate on-demand drug concentration levels exemplify how nanocarriers can be custom designed to meet the distinct pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic needs of individual patients \[[89](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_089)\]. Employing nanocomposites for localized drug delivery, as illustrated by the targeted use of infliximab for inflammatory bowel disease, showcases the potential of nanocarriers to be precisely tailored to decrease systemic exposure while improving locoregional drug administration, in accordance with the patient’s distinct disease phase and biological surroundings \[[90](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_090)\].
    
    Several critical immunological parameters must be taken into account for the customization of nanocarriers, in alignment with patient profiles. Understanding the immunomodulatory effects of nanoparticles is essential, since they can influence drug biodistribution and toxicity, potentially triggering either favorable or unfavorable immune reactions, dictated by the formulation and administration technique. The immune system’s role in the detection and subsequent clearance of nanoparticles can optimize therapeutic efficacy; however, this necessitates comprehensive toxicological evaluations to preclude potential harm \[[91](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_091)\]. Moreover, nanoparticles could play a crucial role in promoting antigen-specific T-cell tolerance within autoimmune diseases, indicating a beneficial method for reintroducing immune tolerance through focused interaction with designated antigen-presenting cells \[[92](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_092)\]. Immune response modulation in nanocarrier design must be taken into consideration, as in biomimetic nanoparticles for cancer immunotherapy, which can enhance the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment \[[93](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_093)\]. Physicochemical characteristics of nucleic acid nanoparticles (NANPs) and delivery devices thereof play an important role in immune response modulation, with predictive resources such as AI\-cell playing an important role in guiding NANP design for the best immunological benefit \[[94](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_094)\]. Dose and route of administration of nanoparticles control antibody response against lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) applied for mRNA delivery, with every route inducing a distinct immune response \[[95](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_095)\]. Nanoparticle surface modification has the potential to enhance their immune-activating profile, modulating protein loading and delivery to target tissues and being safe \[[96](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_096)\]. AI\-driven models have the potential to maximize precision in nanocarrier personalization by incorporating molecular profiling data to stratify patients and forecast drug response, allowing for more personalized treatment for autoimmune and other multifactorial diseases \[[97](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_097)\].
    
    ### 1.4.2 Applications in precision medicine
    
    The recent developments in precision medicine have discovered notable biomarkers that increase the efficacy of AI\-augmented polymer drug delivery systems (DDS) for cancer treatment. They are drug response predictors and putative therapeutic targets, which can be used to design personalized treatment regimens. In hypopharyngeal cancer, four biomarkers – AGR2, PDE4D, NINJ2, and CDC25B – are associated with cellular sensitivity to chemotherapeutic drugs such as docetaxel, cisplatin, and 5-fluorouracil. These biomarkers are drug response predictors and therapeutic targets, enabling precision medicine strategies to chemotherapy in hypopharyngeal cancer patients \[[98](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_098)\]. In drug-resistant cancer, aggregation-induced emission (AIE)-active polymers are promising by regulating redox homeostasis, overcoming barriers to enhance drug accumulation and penetration, thus enhancing therapeutic efficacy \[[99](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_099)\]. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), proteomic profiling and AI technologies have found new biomarkers like AFP, GPC3, and DKK1, involved in dysregulated pathways like Wnt/β-catenin and PI3K/Akt, providing leads for early diagnosis, prognosis, and targeted therapy \[[100](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_100)\]. Dysregulation of the CDK4/6 cell cycle regulatory pathway is a significant feature of pediatric and young adult sarcomas. CDK4/6 inhibition has been a promising therapy, though resistance is a concern, leading to the discovery of new combination therapies to enhance efficacy \[[101](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_101)\]. The integration of AI in bioinformatics has markedly progressed the knowledge surrounding biomarkers tied to CDK4/6 inhibitors, uncovering genes like ERBB2, AKT1, and PIK3CA as fresh targets in breast cancer therapy \[[102](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_102)\]. The fusion of quantitative molecular proteomics, alongside immunology, has highlighted immune checkpoint biomarkers, specifically PD-1/PD-L1, as significant predictors for immunotherapy responses. Moreover, deep learning neural network models have recognized genes such as CCR7 and LGALS1 as critical predictors of immune checkpoint therapy response, thereby enhancing patient stratification \[[103](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_103), [104](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_104)\],.
    
    Ionizable drug delivery frameworks (IDDSs) have revealed considerable potential in alleviating toxicity and boosting nucleic acid delivery. These systems exhibit pH sensitivity, which is particularly advantageous within the acidic milieu of endosomes. Exposure to the reduced pH profile found in endosomes triggers IDDSs to undergo a structural shift that enhances the release of nucleic acids into the cytoplasm, which in turn boosts the success of gene delivery \[[103](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_103), [105](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_105)\]. One significant case of a positive application exists in the management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), an intense genetic illness defined by advancing muscle loss. Established strategies for the delivery of antisense oligonucleotides (AONs) face challenges arising from their vulnerability and inadequate tissue absorption. To address these challenges, hydrogel-forming polymeric carriers have been meticulously engineered. These carriers establish a stable environment for AONs, safeguarding the molecules from degradation and enhancing their uptake within muscle tissue. Consequently, patients afflicted with DMD have reported improved therapeutic outcomes, encompassing enhanced muscle functionality and a deceleration in disease progression \[[106](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_106)\]. Yet another progress in drug formulations that are polymer-derived involves the implementation of ionizable LNPs (iLNPs), which have been adapted for the conveyance of mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. The function of iLNPs to encapsulate, stabilize, and proficiently convey therapeutic agents, including nucleic acids, to designated cells has surfaced as a point of great significance. Their proficiency in stabilizing mRNA against degradation and facilitating cellular uptake has expedited the rapid development of COVID-19 vaccines. Additionally, it has highlighted the prospects of iLNPs for different purposes in gene therapy, targeting the resolution of genetic ailments and cancerous growths \[[107](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_107)\]. Studies have considered DNA nanostructures as multifunctional delivery systems for therapeutic drugs in cancer-related treatments. These tiny structures are uniquely tailored with aptamers, enabling a focused approach to delivering cancer-fighting drugs to tumor cells, thus lowering off-target reactions and boosting the effectiveness of anticancer therapies. For example, the application of DNA nanostructures for the delivery of doxorubicin to cancer cells has resulted in improved tumor suppression while concurrently mitigating side effects \[[108](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_108)\]. Glycopolymers have also been researched for targeted gene delivery, particularly in HCC therapy. Glycopolymers incorporate sugar units that can interact with specific receptors on the liver cell surface. Through this interaction, therapeutic genes can be delivered with high specificity and transfection efficiency and thus render them as promising vectors for HCC gene therapy. In such a case, off-target avoidance and liver cell targeting need to be employed to enable effective gene therapy \[[109](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_109)\].
    
    Polymeric drug delivery systems are a breakthrough approach for the treatment of infectious diseases, leading to maximum therapeutic effectiveness and no antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Polymeric characterization is utilized to ensure maximum bioavailability of antibiotics and site-specific delivery, with the best drug concentration at the site of infection. Fluoroquinolones, encapsulated in polymer-based nanocarriers, have achieved maximum antimicrobial activity against Staphylococcus aureus pathogens through the maintenance of sustained high local concentrations of drugs, reducing opportunities for resistance development \[[110](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_110)\]. Site-specific delivery maximizes efficacy and minimizes systemic exposure, which is vital in minimizing resistance-mediated selective pressure. AI maximizes the potential of these systems through drug combination optimization and dosing regimen optimization. Platforms like IDentif.AI can potentially identify synergistic drug combinations, useful for combating multidrug-resistant infections such as nontuberculous mycobacteria infections \[[111](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_111)\]. AI can predict effective antibiotic combinations, minimizing trial-and-error experimentation and maximizing patient outcomes. Machine learning facilitates treatment optimization by patient history through therapy selection based on reduced probabilities of resistance \[[112](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_112)\]. Personalized therapy maximizes therapy efficacy while minimizing risk of contribution to AMR. Novel polymeric systems like temperature-responsive hydrogels and hyaluronic-acid-based drug delivery systems attain antimicrobial precision of therapy through drug release, in accordance with specific physiological conditions. This has been successful in combating intra-abdominal infections and dermal infections and minimized systemic side effects and maximized efficacy \[[113](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_113), [114](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_114)\]. Sustaining drug concentrations over a long period at infection sites minimizes requirements for high systemic dosages of drugs, reducing the pressure to develop resistance \[[115](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_115)\]. AI maximizes the dosing regimens, especially for multifactorial conditions like sepsis. Algorithms such as the deep deterministic policy gradient help in calculating the optimal dose of antibiotics in real time and deliver precise volumes of medication to combat infection without overexposure. This level of precision optimizes survival and reduces risk of resistance by avoiding suboptimal or excessive dosing \[[116](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_116)\].
    
    Computational modeling that is AI\-based allows the design and optimization of polymeric carriers for the effective delivery of therapeutic agents with minimal side effects. One of the approaches includes peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR-γ) agonist-loaded nanocarriers for inflammatory eye disorders. These formulations enhance drug retention at the target site that suppresses inflammation without inducing cytotoxicity or compromising corneal integrity. Conventional approaches are unable to overcome rapid drug clearance and poor tissue penetration; hence it is a major advancement in ocular drug delivery \[[117](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_117)\]. Polymeric nanoparticles responsive to reactive oxygen species (ROS) have been designed for the treatment of inflammatory skin disorders, which utilize disease-specific oxidative stress to trigger controlled drug release in inflamed tissues, providing localized therapy with minimal systemic exposure \[[118](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_118)\]. AI\-optimized nanocarriers are demonstrating improved drug delivery specificity in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. Dexamethasone-loaded flexible liposome hydrogels have been designed for transdermal delivery, which provides targeted drug release at inflamed joints that minimizes systemic corticosteroid exposure by avoiding immune suppression and metabolic side effects of long-term steroid treatment \[[119](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_119)\]. Poly(ε-caprolactone) nanoparticles have been designed for sustained intra-articular delivery of leflunomide for a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD). By targeting drug action in inflamed joints, these nanoparticles suppress inflammatory markers without inducing systemic toxicity, overcoming a limitation of conventional systemic DMARD administration \[[120](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_120)\]. Advances in polymeric drug delivery include smart colonic delivery systems for inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). These systems utilize pH-sensitive polymer formulations that ensure drug release selectively in the colon, improving therapeutic efficacy and minimizing dosing frequency. Such selectivity maintains drug stability in the gut and minimizes inflammation in other parts of the gastrointestinal tract \[[121](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_121)\]. AI is also driving bio-based polymeric material design at an ever-increasing pace. Bayesian optimization\-based machine learning algorithms efficiently design high-performance, environmentally friendly polymers. These processes accelerate material design, minimize material cost, and maximize mechanical as well as biocompatibility functionalities of the polymer, enabling improved drug delivery platforms \[[122](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_122)\].
    
    The drug delivery strategies for neurodegenerative diseases by improving bioavailability, targeting specificity, and penetration through biological barriers such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB) are transformed by the application of polymer formulations. These formulations employ polymeric nanocarriers to provide controlled and sustained release of the drug, which results in enhanced therapeutic effects and minimized systemic side effects. Strategies involving AI have played a key role in the optimization of these formulations for enhanced penetration through the BBB and controlled release of the drug at the diseased neuronal sites \[[123](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_123), [124](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_124)\]. Biodegradable polymeric carriers provide sustained and prolonged release of therapeutic agents. These carriers increase the half-life of the drug and induce nerve regeneration and functional recovery, which is essential in diseases with neuronal damage such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases. Research shows that polymeric drug delivery systems can improve neuroprotection by stabilizing and prolonging the activity of neurotrophic factors and anti-inflammatory drugs and preventing neuronal degeneration \[[125](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_125)\]. Machine learning algorithms optimize these polymer-based systems by revealing molecular transport mechanisms that can be optimized to enhance drug permeability and ion selectivity through polymeric membranes. It also helps in the selection of effective polymer compositions to penetrate the BBB while maintaining drug stability and activity in the central nervous system \[[126](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_126)\]. Optimization, which involves AI, helps in reduced trial-and-error experiments and effective neurotherapeutic formulations, which also are formulated at a very faster rate. Interpenetrating polymer networks (IPNs) render drug delivery by responding to external stimuli such as pH and temperature. The networks provide site-specific and sustained release of the drug that provides precise modulation of therapeutic action based on pathophysiological conditions in the brain. IPNs have also been found to target dysregulated disease pathways of neurodegenerative diseases that include chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, effectively. They help in facilitating co-delivery of drugs, improving biodistribution and synergistic therapeutic effects, which leads to more comprehensive neuroprotective effects \[[127](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_127)\]. Nanocarrier systems such as cell-derived nanovesicles and exosomes are currently the cutting-edge platforms for targeted brain drug delivery. These carriers are naturally biocompatible and can penetrate the BBB, making them effective vehicles to deliver therapeutic agents to diseased neurons \[[128](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_128)\]. Predictive modelling, in assistance with AI, optimizes their potential in precision medicine that allows treatments to be designed according to patient-specific needs. Drug design involving AI has made it possible to design polymer formulations with both synthetic and phytochemical compounds that target multiple pathogenic mechanisms at once. These formulations enhance neuroprotection by stabilizing antioxidants, modulating neuro inflammation, and enhancing neuronal survival pathways. By combining AI with polymer science, scientists can screen hundreds of thousands of potential formulations quickly and optimize those with the highest therapeutic potential \[[124](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_124)\]. Optimization through AI continues to optimize the design and application of polymer-based drug delivery systems and hence the future of neurotherapeutic interventions will be marked by continued advances in precision medicine, promising more effective and personalized interventions for disabling neurodegenerative diseases \[[129](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_ref_129)\]. A summary of some applications of AI in precision medicine is presented in [Table 1.1](#chapter-001.xhtml#b_9783111681870-001_tab_001).

    ## 1.5 Conclusion
    
    The synergy of AI and polymeric nanotechnology is a revolutionary strategy for drug discovery and targeted delivery by overcoming the limitations faced by conventional therapeutics. AI data analytics, predictive modeling, and algorithms facilitate the simple fabrication of polymeric nanocarriers. This technology offers solutions to the challenges of lack of bioavailability, off-targeting, non-patient-specific treatment tailoring, and most importantly, enables precise control of dosage. AI optimizes the design of biocompatible polymers so that the properties of the polymer can be tailored to match the needs of particular diseases and the individuals affected by them. This customization brings about greater encapsulation efficiency, improved drug release kinetics, precise targeting of diseased tissues, and in general, enhanced therapeutic effects with fewer side effects. The use of AI in the discovery of medicines via polymer nanotechnology overcomes the issues involved in long prototype and refinement procedures with polymeric nanocarrier systems. This substantially reduces the development time required and promotes the development of precision medicine such that all approaches to treatment are tailored to each person’s individual genetic, molecular, and physiologic make-up. Possible applications range from cancer treatments to infectious disease therapies, providing more efficient treatment opportunities. In summary, the union of AI with polymeric nanotechnology is a major breakthrough in medicine. With the integration of sophisticated computational approaches and novel material sciences, the method holds high levels of precise, patient-specific therapeutic interventions. As AI improves, its conjunction with polymer nanotechnology will spearhead the future of pharmaceuticals, transforming the diagnosis, treatment, and control of disease to better the patients’ quality of life across the world.

    # Chapter 2 Machine learning applications in material science: unveiling innovative solutions
    
    Leandro Rodrigues Oviedo Maurício Dalla Costa Rodrigues da Silva Pâmela Cristine Ladwig Muraro Raisi Natalia Lenz Baldez Tiago Moreno Volkmer William Leonardo da Silva 
    
    **Acknowledgment:** Authors would also like to thank the Federal University of Health Sciences of Porto Alegre (UFCSPA), Technological University of Uruguay (UTEC), Federal University of Pelotas (UFPEL) and Franciscan University (UFN) for their support.
    
    #### Abstract
    
    Since the twentieth century, polymers have transformed modern society due to their versatility, durability, flexibility, and cost-effectiveness, making them suitable for industrial applications, such as packaging, electronics, automotive, medical devices, and consumer goods. Precise control over polymer synthesis is crucial to ensure consistency and tailored properties for specific applications. The prediction of polymeric properties, such as flame resistance, mechanical stability, and thermal stability, is crucial for complying with industry standards and promoting safety and technological innovation. However, optimizing synthesis and investigating properties at lab scale is time-consuming and costly, which emphasizes the need for computational methods to overcome these drawbacks and fasten commercialization. Artificial intelligence algorithms have been promising in materials science due to their good performance in materials synthesis optimization. Thus, this chapter provides an overview of the main machine learning (ML) and deep learning algorithms used to optimize polymer synthesis, with a focus on the tuning of polymeric properties and investigating durability. Moreover, supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms are discussed as well as their main advantages/challenges in polymer science. Thereafter, the main assays for polymer characterization are also discussed. These assays include X-ray diffraction, Raman, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, which can be associated with ML algorithms (e.g., convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, especially long short-term memory ), reinforcement learning, and computer vision. These approaches are considered promising for the design of optimized polymers to predict their degradation rates/recycling efficiency and can be helpful in classification tasks (non-compostable and compostable polymers).
    
    Keywords:  Artificial intelligence (AI),  machine learning (ML),  deep learning (DL),  polymer,  artificial neural network (ANN),  
    
    ## 2.1 Introduction to machine learning paper in polymer science
    
    Polymers, including microplastics, are ubiquitous in the environment \[[1](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_001)\]. The term “polymer” refers to a wide variety of materials that are constituted of extended molecular chains formed by the repetition of monomeric units \[[2](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_002)\].
    
    Polymeric materials are present in almost every aspect of our lives, ranging from common synthetic plastics (e.g., polystyrene) to natural biopolymers (e.g., DNA and proteins). Polymers exhibit mechanical strength, flexibility, high-temperature resistance, and electrical conductivity, which are determined by their unique molecular composition and structure \[[3](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_003), [4](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_004)\]. Its remarkable properties (mechanical, chemical, physical, and biological) provide a wide range of applications in areas such as biomedicine, chemistry, and materials science \[[5](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_005)\].
    
    Due to their characteristics, polymers are widely used in various areas of industry, including packaging, manufacturing, textiles, automotive, medical, and electronics. An example of a polymer widely and historically used in industry is polypropylene. It has been used as a material with dielectric properties in high-energy-density capacitors, due to its high self-compensation in cases of failure and low production costs \[[6](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_006)\].
    
    The synthesis/development of new polymers, combined with the existence of a wide range of polymers, requires a comprehensive understanding and documentation of the physical and mechanical properties associated with these materials \[[6](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_006)\]. Using traditional experimental methods, it is time-consuming and costly to search for polymers that satisfy specific properties for different applications. However, their exploration can be aided and increased by computationally and data-driven design algorithms.
    
    Machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence (AI), is a powerful tool for prediction of material properties, synthesis optimization, and pattern recognition within experimental data, especially when working with large datasets \[[7](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_007)\]. These algorithms can be used to understand and construct the intricate relationships between input and output results \[[8](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_008)\].
    
    In recent years, ML and AI have become increasingly popular in materials science \[[9](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_009)\]. The techniques provide viable solutions for prognosticating the properties of polymers and have demonstrated significant impacts in several areas \[[10](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_010)\]. This technique allows, for example, to establish a direct correspondence between the characteristics of fibers and the properties of composites, among other diverse applications, including catalyst design, design and creation of new materials, and drug research \[[11](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_011)\].
    
    It is worth highlighting that neural network-based algorithms often require large datasets for training/learning process. For this reason, the learning process can be computationally intensive or, in other words, expensive. When dealing with limited datasets, learning algorithms such as regression trees, Gaussian process regression (GPR), support vector regression (SVR), or kernel ridge regression are more suitable for certain applications \[[12](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_012)\].
    
    In materials science, the direct use of polymers to train ML models is not practicable at present. Therefore, it is essential to represent polymer structures in a way that is easily comprehensible by the machine (computer) \[[13](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_013)\]. In this field, empirical methods and simulations were used to develop and meet the demand for new materials \[[14](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_014)\]. This approach requires significant instruments and often involves getting certain advantages and skills.
    
    ML has enabled the creation of new chemical potentials for polymers, the development of membrane materials, the prediction of polymer properties with defined sequences, the design of bioplastics, and the optimization of 3D printing.
    
    Despite these advances, the field still presents challenges, unique to polymer science. Different from other materials, the structure of polymers is stochastic rather than fixed, which makes the representation of polymers in ML algorithms challenging \[[15](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_015)\]. Defining all atoms in complex polymers is not feasible due to the high computational demand of input representations needed for the use of the technique. An option is to, instead of directly using all sequenced atoms in a polymer chain as a source of feature representations, consider alternatives such as the use of chemical compounds or functional groups that may be more valuable and practical for representing polymers \[[16](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_016)\].
    
    The field of polymer science faces major challenges when it comes to using ML in materials prediction. Databases of polymeric materials are not easily accessible to the public. Many of the essential measurements require instruments manufactured by companies with limited open interfaces/models. This makes it difficult to create databases and nearly impossible to integrate these devices into high-performance systems \[[17](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_017)\].
    
    In short, too much research has been developed to better represent the polymeric structure and to incorporate expert knowledge about polymers into ML algorithms. The future of the technique is promising for polymeric materials, but further research still needs to be encouraged in this area.
    
    ## 2.2 Prediction and optimization of physicochemical properties
    
    Comprehension of the physical and chemical properties of polymeric materials is essential for their effective application in various fields. Polymer properties are highly dependent on the structure of the polymer chains, molecular weight, and physical structure, affecting chemical, mechanical and thermal properties \[[18](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_018)\]. The relationship between structure and properties helps in designing polymers for specific applications, ensuring their optimal performance and durability \[[19](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_019)\]. Predicting polymer properties is therefore crucial, not only for advancing material science but also for enabling the design of next-generation functional materials \[[20](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_020)\].
    
    Traditional approaches for polymer property estimation rely heavily on experimental measurements and computational simulations such as molecular dynamics (MD), for example, LAMMPS \[[21](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_021)\], GROMACS \[[22](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_022)\], NAMD \[[23](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_023)\], and DL\_POLY \[[24](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_024)\], which are frequently employed to estimate a wide range of polymeric material properties such as crystallization, polymer drug uptake, structural properties, reverse osmosis membranes \[[21](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_021), [22](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_022), [23](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_023), [24](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_024)\], while Monte Carlo based methods such as DL\_MONTE \[[25](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_025)\] and Cassandra \[[26](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_026)\] are used for gas transport and dilation resistance of separation membranes \[[25](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_025), [26](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_026)\]. At the quantum level, packages like Quantum ESPRESSO \[[27](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_027)\] and VASP \[[28](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_028)\] are commonly used for DFT and first principles approach.
    
    Even with all the advancements and consistency of experimental or simulation-based methods, they often require extensive property measurements, which are both time-consuming and expensive \[[29](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_029), [30](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_030)\]. Hence, there is a pressing need for innovative methodologies to accelerate polymers’ design process without compromising accuracy \[[31](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_031)\]. To address this gap, Machine Learning (ML) has emerged as an informatic innovative tool to analyze, predict, and optimize polymer properties with remarkable accuracy \[[32](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_032)\]. However, the complex and periodic nature of polymer structures presents difficulties in data representation \[[33](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_033)\], while the lack of standardized, high-quality datasets limits model generalization \[[34](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_034)\]. Another challenge is that many ML models function as black-box optimization tools, raising concerns about interpretability and experimental validation. Therefore, overcoming these challenges requires collaborative efforts in data curation, model explainability, and integration with traditional simulation methods \[[35](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_035), [36](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_036)\].
    
    ### 2.2.1 Polymer featurization
    
    Since machine learning algorithms require numerical data, it is essential to convert these chemical groups into machine-readable representations that can be used to build predictive models, which can be used to predict and/or optimize polymeric properties \[[37](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_037)\].
    
    One of the most common strategies for transforming categorical data into a mathematical description suitable for ML models is One-hot Encoding (OHE) \[[38](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_038)\], in which the polymer sequence is transformed into a binary vector, allowing efficient processing of categorical features by ML algorithms \[[38](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_038), [39](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_039)\]. OHE can also be applied to SMILES strings, which are text-based representations of molecular structures. These strings are often used to describe small molecules or repeating units in polymers. By converting SMILES into vector formats, such as binary images, they become more accessible for machine learning models to work with \[[40](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_040), [41](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_041), [42](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_042)\].
    
    Property coloring offers another approach by representing polymers as three-dimensional arrays, with each dimension corresponding to specific chemical properties of the monomeric units. These arrays are then processed through filters, generating complex, image-like structures that are well-suited for feature extraction in machine learning models \[[43](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_043)\]. Another advanced technique, known as the chemical tree, leverages atomic-level descriptions to define the chemical composition of polymer subunits. This method organizes polymers into hierarchical tree structures that encapsulate both monomer-level and atomic-level information \[[44](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_044), [45](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_045)\].
    
    Autoencoding represents another powerful featurization technique. This neural network-based approach converts discrete molecular representations, such as SMILES strings, into continuous variables within a latent space. The encoder component performs dimensionality reduction, while the decoder reconstructs the original molecular structure from the compressed form, providing compact, yet meaningful features for ML tasks \[[46](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_046), [47](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_047), [48](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_048)\]. Lastly, motif-based fingerprinting extracts molecular features by examining the number and connectivity of specific atoms within a molecular structure. By identifying recurring chemical motifs and leveraging principles of chemical bonding, this method generates rich, descriptive representations of polymers \[[49](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_049), [50](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_050)\].
    
    ### 2.2.2 ML for properties prediction
    
    Machine learning algorithms are typically divided into the following categories: supervised, semisupervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning \[[51](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_051)\].
    
    #### 2.2.2.1 Unsupervised machine learning models
    
    Unsupervised models have emerged as essential tools in polymer research, offering novel approaches for identifying and classifying polymers without relying on labeled datasets \[[52](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_052)\]. It is primarily used for exploration, clustering, dimensionality reduction, and anomaly detection. Methods such as principal component analysis, diffusion maps, self-organizing maps, and autoencoder networks have been successfully used to distinguish different polymer states and configuration states, and enabled the detection and quantification of complex structural features such as voids and grains \[[53](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_053), [54](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_054), [55](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_055)\].
    
    #### 2.2.2.2 Supervised machine learning models
    
    In supervised ML models, the data used for training and testing are labeled with property values. After the featurization process to ensure that the data are in a format suitable for the algorithms, the dataset is typically divided into training data (usually 70–80% of dataset) and test data subsets. During the training phase, several regression models such as random forest, gradient boosting, XGBoost, bagging regressor, AdaBoost can be employed to learn from the inputs and, as an output, predict the physical and chemical properties of polymeric materials \[[32](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_032)\]. To improve predictive accuracy and prevent issues like bias, underfitting, or overfitting, each model relies on a specific set of hyperparameters, adjustable settings defined before training starts. These hyperparameters can be tuned either manually or through automated methods such as grid search and random search. These tools systematically or randomly explore different combinations to identify the configuration that yields the best model performance \[[54](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_054)\]. To assess model performance, commonly used evaluation metrics include the determination coefficient (*R*²), mean absolute error (MAE), mean percentage error, mean squared error (MSE), and root MSE. Once training is complete, the best metric values for each feature across all models are recorded and analyzed using graphical tools, allowing for a clear comparison and identification of the most effective machine learning model \[[55](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_055)\].
    
    #### 2.2.2.3 Semisupervised machine learning models
    
    This approach integrates both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to train predictive models. The input data may originate from a single dataset or from multiple datasets \[[56](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_056)\]. Semisupervised regression presents a promising strategy for predicting labels on unlabeled data, while also estimating label confidence – information that can be used to expand the training set and improve model accuracy \[[57](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_057)\].
    
    #### 2.2.2.4 Reinforcement machine learning models
    
    Reinforcement learning is a class of algorithms that uses machines and software agents to automatically determine optimal behavior within a specific context to improve overall efficiency \[[51](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_051)\]. These algorithms rely on iterative interactions between agents and their environments, aiming to maximize a defined reward signal. Techniques such as Markov decision processes and active learning exemplify this approach \[[58](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_058)\]. Active learning is valuable in scenarios with limited labeled data. Rather than relying solely on available examples, the model actively selects the most informative new instances, known as queries, to suggest the “next-best experiment.” These selected examples are then incorporated into the training set, and the model is retrained. This cycle continues, allowing the model to improve more rapidly by concentrating on the most valuable data points \[[58](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_058), [59](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_ref_059)\].
    
    ### 2.2.3 Machine learning studies examples
    
    To enable comparison across studies utilizing ML to predict the mechanical and physicochemical properties of polymers, [Table 2.1](#chapter-002.xhtml#b_9783111681870-002_tab_001) provides a summary of key information extracted from the selected literature, including the models, data sources, predicted properties, and *R*² values.
