    # Chapter 11 Discovering new frontiers: material explorations with AI and polymers
    
    Tamanna Rai Rishabha Malviya 
    
    #### Abstract
    
    Artificial intelligence (AI) has been a key tool in many fields, including the creation and development of polymer materials, since the start of the digital revolution. This chapter thoroughly analyzes the AI approaches used in this setting, including materials informatics. To explore new horizons in material design and innovation, it focuses on the synergistic integration of AI with polymer science. Additionally, the chapter discusses the application of machine learning (ML) to the development and identification of polymer materials. Lastly, the obstacles and potential for ML future development in polymer materials are suggested.
    
    Keywords:  Artificial intelligence,  machine learning,  polymer science,  property prediction,  deep learning,  smart material,  polymer synthesis,  
    
    ## 11.1 Introduction
    
    The advancement of machine learning (ML)-based approaches has resulted in the development of cutting-edge methods in scientific fields such as materials science and polymer engineering. ML has recently advanced materials science by utilizing computer algorithms that improve research, awareness, exploration, and modeling \[[1](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_001)\]. When combined with human ingenuity, these algorithms can greatly aid in the discovery and innovation of new materials for the next innovations \[[2](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_002)\]. Appropriate design of experiment (DoE) approaches are crucial for the methodical exploration of the design space and the required attributes when designing new materials \[[3](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_003)\]. This frequently entails choices about a variety of topics, such as system configurations, operating circumstances, and material qualities. The experiential method is used in classical design approaches, which poses some challenges \[[4](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_004)\]. Primarily, due to their exclusive provision of point-wise evaluation, the relationships between the dependent and independent variables sometimes lack a definitive mathematical representation and are termed “black-box functions” \[[5](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_005)\]. Secondly, the design space frequently encompasses numerous independent factors, leading to an extensive array of potential combinations. A detailed search rapidly becomes impractical as dimensionality increases \[[6](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_006)\].
    
    ML seeks to create and evaluate statistical algorithms that acquire knowledge from data and utilize this knowledge on novel, unobserved data, hence enabling independent task performance without direct programming \[[7](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_007)\]. This advancement functions as a robust instrument for evaluating current polymer materials and identifying novel ones, signifying a substantial transition from conventional methods that depend largely on individual expertise and frequently necessitate considerable time, occasionally extending over decades, from initial experimentation to market introduction \[[8](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_008)\].
    
    This chapter distinguishes itself by focusing on ML applications in the formulation and optimization of specific polymer classes, addressing unique issues and customized ML methodologies for each. This work distinguishes itself from broader reviews by focusing on the actual application of ML in expediting the design process, forecasting material attributes, and optimizing formulations to attain desired performance more effectively. Moreover, it examines future trends and obstacles, offering a balanced evaluation that considers both current and prospective limitations, a topic often overlooked in the literature \[[9](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_009)\]. This chapter claims the importance of ML in boosting polymer material innovation by highlighting the shortcomings of traditional experimentation and time-consuming simulations in polymer design \[[10](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_010)\].
    
    ## 11.2 Fundamental process for machine learning\-enhanced polymer development
    
    A genetic algorithm (GA) was employed to construct numerous polymer networks with specified attributes \[[11](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_011)\]. Subsequently, ML techniques were applied to calculate the characteristics of polymers and conduct design studies. These models pertain to property prediction or new material discovery and follow the subsequent procedures, as shown in [Figure 11.1](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_fig_001).
    
    *   Stage 1: Acquiring molecular structures from literature or accessible databases.
        
    *   Stage 2: Molecules are fingerprinted into shapes that computers can recognize. To be more specific, this involves turning these three-dimensional chemical shapes into tensors.
        
    *   Stage 3: Researchers can develop a structure-property prediction algorithm by selecting an appropriate ML framework and entering molecular data.
        
    *   Stage 4: Selecting a suitable ML model to build novel compounds and using the framework to predict features in Stages 1–3.
        
    *   Stage 5: Examining these new compounds using domain expertise to confirm that the selected samples adhere to essential chemical principles and can be synthesized. Ultimately, one can acquire the requisite polymer \[[12](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_012), [13](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_013), [14](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_014), [15](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_015)\].
        
    
    ![Figure 11.1: Illustrates the basic flowchart for artificial polymer discovery.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-011_fig_001.jpg)
    
    Figure 11.1: Illustrates the basic flowchart for artificial polymer discovery.
    
    ## 11.3 Data collection
    
    Data is crucial when using ML to research polymer membranes. The efficacy of ML models is greatly impacted by their accuracy and the volume of data used to train them \[[16](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_016)\]. One of the most significant obstacles in constructing strong ML models is the limited availability of data, particularly in terms of maintaining superior quality \[[17](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_017)\]. Inadequate, low-quality datasets do not accurately reflect the complete diversity of the overall data population, potentially leading to biased forecasts. Training with limited datasets frequently leads to overfitting; thus, the model captures noise instead of the expected basic patterns. As a result, it loses its ability to extrapolate to new, unknown facts \[[18](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_018)\]. By reducing bias, improving feature representation, and giving models more ability to make predictions across the training data, large, exceptional datasets can help mitigate these disadvantages \[[19](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_019)\]. The absence of clearly defined criteria for identifying low-quality data complicates the assessment of data trustworthiness. Verifying the data can enhance the dataset’s quality by detecting outliers or inaccurate data points \[[20](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_020)\].
    
    Making sure that the dataset contains at least ten times as many data points as there are input variable types is a widely used strategy to avoid overfitting and improve model dependability. The following subsections outline common data collection methods \[[21](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_021)\].
    
    ### 11.3.1 The compilation of datasets from literature
    
    The comprehensive global citation database “Web of Science” contains about one million papers related to the term “polymer” \[[22](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_022)\]. Furthermore, given that polymer research is an expeditiously advancing discipline, the quantity of accessible polymers will perpetually increase \[[23](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_023)\]. This technique has been accepted by a multiplicity of academics since it alleviates the restrictions of the current information system and allows researchers to engineer particular polymers \[[24](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_024)\]. The drawback of this strategy is that dataset creation is labor-intensive, and the data points may be fewer than those from existing databases \[[25](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_025)\]. Recently, researchers developed a mechanical data extraction approach based on language processing algorithms and ML. This could be an excellent technique to avoid the challenges associated with gathering datasets based on books \[[26](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_026)\]. The fact that almost all research studies only report selected findings, meaning that only partial information is available, is another issue with this data collection process \[[27](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_027)\]. Consequently, these data do not conform to the Gaussian distribution criteria and may lead to overfitting in ML models.
    
    ### 11.3.2 Compilation of data from theoretical models or scientific computations
    
    Academics frequently utilize scientific computational techniques or conceptual frameworks when they cannot locate the necessary details in current databases or publications \[[28](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_028)\]. For example, Liu and Cao derived 11 pertinent parameters to predict glass transition temperature using density functional theory (DFT). Using a molecular dynamics (MD) model and ML, Zhu et al. created 300 different kinds of single-chain polymer compounds with high heat conductivity. Using the ADAPT toolkit, researchers identified 100–300 relevant parameters for employing ML to predict the temperature at which glass transitions \[[29](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_029)\].
    
    ### 11.3.3 Data preprocessing and feature engineering
    
    After being collected, the initial information needs to be cleaned up and set up before it can be used in ML models or for more research. A lot of things go into preprocessing or the preparation of data. Data cleaning includes finding and fixing mistakes, getting rid of duplicates, and getting rid of outliers from a set of data \[[30](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_030)\]. This is done to make sure that the data is accurate and of higher quality, and that there are no flaws. Adding new numbers to a set of data to fill in missing ones is called data imputation \[[31](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_031)\]. Data retrieved from the literature frequently contains datasets with missing values for specific variables, necessitating this procedure. Due to its intrinsic chemical and physical properties, raw data is sometimes used by researchers, while others opt to use mean or median values for data calculation \[[32](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_032)\]. Data normalization is the process of changing the distribution of data so that it is suitable for ML analysis. This means changing the data to fit a normal distribution and normalizing it to have a standard deviation of one and a median of zero \[[33](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_033)\]. It is essential to translate categorical features into a format that is interpretable by computers, as ML models generally cannot directly analyze categorical data (e.g., types of solutes, polymers, or solvents). Examples of these computer-readable formats include one-hot encoding, label encoding, and binary encoding \[[34](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_034)\].
    
    ## 11.4 Fingerprinting
    
    During this stage, scientists transform 3D molecules into scalars or tensors, facilitating computer interpretation and subsequent processing. We acknowledge that several fingerprinting methodologies are discussed separately below \[[35](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_035)\].
    
    ### 11.4.1 Line notation
    
    The Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) is a commonly utilized format for depicting molecular structures \[[36](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_036)\]. SMILES strings comprise alphanumeric characters that denote bonds and atoms within a molecule \[[37](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_037)\]. They contain information about the molecule’s atoms, linkages, rings, and branches. SMILES strings are notable for their direct usefulness as descriptors in ML models and their capacity to be transformed into alternative descriptors \[[38](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_038)\]. As a result, SMILES strings are crucial for molecular expression in a way that ML algorithms can understand which streamlines the application of ML to the creation of polymers.
    
    ### 11.4.2 Morgan fingerprinting
    
    Rogers and Hahn developed Morgan fingerprinting as a re-execution of the extended connectivity fingerprint (ECEP). Each monomer can have its distinct sequential atom numbering obtained using this method. Three essential steps make up this method. First, each atom in the monomer is assigned an integer value. Second, the unique identification number of each atom is updated to match that of its neighbors (see Figure 11.2) \[[39](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_039)\]. In this method, each repeat generates an identifier that represents progressively bigger spherical components encircling the central atom. Third, to generate a single representative, identical attributes are eliminated \[[40](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_040)\]. Morgan fingerprinting may be a more effective approach to display 3D structure than linear notation encoding since it can describe each atom and its neighbors. This strategy was also employed in numerous investigations. To put it into practice, use the open-source cheminformatics software RDKit \[[41](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_041)\].
    
    ![Figure 11.2: Diagrammatic representation of Morgan fingerprinting.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-011_fig_002.jpg)
    
    Figure 11.2: Diagrammatic representation of Morgan fingerprinting.
    
    ## 11.5 Machine learning algorithm
    
    The ML approach aims to establish a connection between the fingerprinted input and the target property, which is an effective substitute for predicting the target feature \[[42](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_042)\]. Currently, the model is constructed using both linear and nonlinear regression techniques. The most widely used techniques are kernel-based regression and artificial neural networks (ANNs). Below is a brief description of various techniques \[[43](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_043)\].
    
    ### 11.5.1 Regression model and nonlinear regression algorithms
    
    The linear regression algorithm was one of the original and most basic approaches, representing the desired characteristic as a linear function using fingerprints. These models fail to adjust for the nonlinear relationship between descriptions and qualities, limiting their predictive effectiveness \[[44](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_044)\]. The so-called “Kern trick” is often used to solve this problem in complex regressions. Kernel functions, such as polynomial kernels and radial basis functions, translate data into a higher-dimensional feature space. In linear regression, this is used in place of the original fingerprint x \[[45](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_045)\]. In the original feature space, this process leads to a nonlinear regression. Some kernel-based methods that have been used are Gaussian process regression (GPR), support vector machine (SVM) and kernel ridge regression (KRR) \[[46](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_046)\]. For example, KRR has been used to predict the features of polymers using extensive DFT calculations \[[47](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_047)\]. To expedite the search for high-quality polymers and determine their dielectric constant at various frequencies, particle swarm optimization (PSO) and interval support vector regression were suggested by Yin et al. This study uses the PSO method to enhance the SVM hyper-parameters \[[48](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_048)\].
    
    ### 11.5.2 Random forests
    
    This approach skillfully handles the complex interaction of attributes by combining a variety of decision trees. The maximum allowable depth for all trees and the total number of trees in the forest were two important factors that were adjusted to enhance their performance \[[49](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_049)\].
    
    ### 11.5.3 Gradient boosting machines (GBMs)
    
    Methods like LightGBM and XGBoost were applied to improve prediction accuracy. These models are resistant to overfitting and able to handle large datasets, as they repair faults from earlier rounds \[[50](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_050)\].
    
    ### 11.5.4 Graph convolutional neural network
    
    As previously mentioned, molecular graphs can only use graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) to predict properties. Convolution and pooling are the two ways that GCNN differs from CNN \[[51](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_051)\]. The GCNN kernel is impacted by its surroundings, whereas the CNN kernel has a standard 2D receptive field and moves at a regular Euclidean distance. Second, CNN polls uniformly in a 2D grid, but GCNN polls no uniformly in its surroundings \[[52](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_052)\]. Complex network connection in polymer graphs is an example of a strange area that GCNN can handle because it has two unique properties. A study that employed GCNN to identify the locations of interactions between protein kinase inhibitors found that the accuracy was 86% (Wang et al., 2015) \[[53](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_053)\]. When Tao et al. utilized GCNN to predict a photopolymer’s glass transition temperature; their model was accurate up to 79.18% of the time \[[54](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_054)\]. Altae-Tran et al. employed GCNN in their study to accomplish one-shot acquiring knowledge, and their model performs well in small molecule prediction \[[55](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_055)\]. When Aldephi et al. used the modified GCNN, they looked at the link after polymerization and came up with a new network called wD-MPNN, which seemed to work better than the old GCNN \[[56](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_056)\].
    
    ### 11.5.5 The ANN and the deep neural network
    
    Many years of work have gone into making ANN and deep neural networks (CNN) that work like the brain to learn the connections between different traits and descriptions by doing things over and over again. The output layer displays how well the potential polymers function, while the hidden layers demonstrate the connections between the input and output layers \[[57](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_057)\]. To extract significant features from the input layer and further simplify the features, CNN adds additional standard and pool layers. The convolutional layers are made up of trainable filters that perform distinct convolutions across the entire input. This allows local characteristics to be extracted \[[58](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_058)\]. Pooling layers further reduce feature dimensions by pooling sub regions into a single result. Maximum pooling is the most prevalent type of pooling. When compared to completely linked layers, conventional and pool layers have significantly less buried neurons. This allows networks to go much deeper \[[59](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_059)\]. ML models for the appropriate choice of thermal conductivity, glass transmission temperature, and polymer solvent pairings were created using NNs. A binary classification neural network (NN) model that can determine whether a solvent is suitable for a polymer or not was trained using 11,958 pairs of polymers and good solvents and 8,469 pairs of polymers and nonsolvents to identify the best polymer-solvent pairs. To forecast how thermally conductive polymers will be, we used a CNN trained on thermal conductivities found by traditional MD models. Wei et al. developed a CNN model using 2D cross-sectional photos of polymer composites, which has been shown to accurately forecast how well materials transport heat \[[60](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_060)\].
    
    ### 11.5.6 Decision tree
    
    To help in decision-making, decision trees employ a framework similar to a tree to foretell potential outcomes. It has also been widely utilized for polymer discovery because to its easy understanding ability and reliance on graphical depiction \[[61](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_061)\]. Information gain, gradient boosting, and a variety of other methods have been used to construct decision trees. Li et al. predicted how hydrogels self-assemble using logistic regression, decision trees, and gradient boosting, which may be useful in biomedical settings like cell culture \[[62](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_062)\]. Bhowmik et al. utilized decision trees and principal component analysis (PCA) to predict the specific heat of polymers \[[63](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_063)\]. Kumar et al. separated ribonucleoprotein absorption, toxicity, and editing rates into high and low groups using random forest \[[64](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_064)\].
    
    ### 11.5.7 Variational autoencoders (VAEs)
    
    We looked into the hidden space of polymer structures to come up with different design choices. VAEs used a probabilistic approach to model complex distributions and come up with new polymer options that met certain criteria \[[65](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_065)\].
    
    ## 11.6 Polymer design algorithms
    
    Upon completion of training, the polymer replacement models can be employed to accelerate the discovery of novel polymers. Here are two distinct approaches. The first approach employs predictions to identify candidates that meet specific property requirements. In contrast, the second approach uses generative and genetic models to directly produce desirable candidates \[[66](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_066)\].
    
    ### 11.6.1 Enumeration
    
    Artificial intelligence methodologies are frequently employed to expedite the systematic design and advancement of innovative materials. These technologies operate by effectively exploring a designated chemical area \[[67](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_067)\]. The ML models we’ve already talked about are used to guess the properties of a big group of possible polymers that are listed according to a physical or chemical scheme. The process of reducing the list according to specific screening criteria comes next \[[68](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_068)\]. In the end, a ranked list of qualified candidates for the objective application is eventually generated. The first possibilities could be synthetic polymers that have already been made, or they could be hypothetical polymers that have been made by humans or machines, showing the trends in a way that looks like “Ashby plots” of different ML-predicted features for tens of thousands of known or synthesizable polymers \[[69](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_069)\]. It is possible to choose different combinations of properties based on the needs of specific use \[[70](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_070)\]. For example, polymers with a high glass transition temperature, a high dielectric constant, and a big band gap can withstand temperature extremes. However, the polymeric electrolytes used in Li-ion batteries must have the proper band gap, electron affinity, and ionization energy. Conversely, gas permeability and selection must be precisely calibrated for polymer membranes \[[71](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_071)\].
    
    ### 11.6.2 Evolutionary strategy (genetic algorithm GA)
    
    One term for GA’s underlying principle is “natural selection.” It is simple to treat polymers with GA due to their inherent structure. Polymers consist of several chemical units that are covalently bound to one another. The characteristics of a polymer’s chemical components determine the material’s final characteristics \[[72](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_072)\]. To find new potential polymers with the desired characteristics, the GA method employs a sequence of crossover, mutation, and selection procedures \[[73](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_073)\]. To begin, a large number of polymers are generated at random from a pool of monomers using procedures such as crossover, pruning, mixing, and mutation, which alter the chemical building blocks of the monomers. This process is repeated until a significant number of progeny polymers are obtained \[[74](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_074)\]. The top candidates for the next generation of polymers are chosen based on a user-defined objective score that takes into account their ideal features. This GA cycle is repeated until a sufficient number of candidates possessing the necessary attributes are identified \[[75](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_075)\]. GA has been used for more than just finding polymers. It has also been applied to solve problems in materials science, such as uncovering hidden links between material properties and creating functional forms of interatomic potentials. The objective function being evaluated during the selection step is an important part of the GA design scheme. This step has been a big problem for finding new polymers because figuring out properties through tests or calculations is very expensive and takes a long time. However, new, cost-effective, and accurate polymer property models have made this feasible \[[76](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_076)\]. It is now possible to compute the target function in a fraction of a second. This advancement enables the GA approach to go well beyond preestablished candidate sets and genuinely investigate a very rich chemical polymer space. Additionally, polymers that concurrently meet several property criteria might be targeted by establishing a property-weighted goal function \[[77](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_077)\].
    
    ## 11.7 Application
    
    ### 11.7.1 Polymer electrolytes design for Li-ion batteries
    
    Rechargeable Li-ion batteries are now commonly employed in a variety of industries, including microelectronics and airplanes. Increasingly, people are interested in developing new, superior solid polymer electrolyte materials because they are required in industry \[[78](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_078)\]. For Li-ion batteries to perform at their best, the polymer solutions should exhibit high ionic conductivity, high Li-ion transference, a low glass transition temperature, and a wide electrochemical stability window. Experiments to identify the best electrolytes take a lot of time, so data-driven aided polymer design methods are a great way to save time \[[79](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_079)\]. For instance, to assist with coarse-grained MD simulations, Wang et al. used ML to develop novel polymer solutions with strong ionic conductivity \[[80](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_080)\].
    
    ### 11.7.2 Rational design of polymer dielectrics
    
    The ability of a polymer to polarize in an electric field is determined by its dielectric constant. For electronics, both extremely high and low dielectric constant polymers are required \[[81](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_081)\]. In an integrated circuit (IC), low dielectric polymers are used as insulation to keep signal-carrying wires apart and to prevent coupling between metal lines that are close to one another \[[82](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_082)\]. Conversely, high dielectric polymers are essential for semiconductors and high-density energy storage devices. Many well-known polymers have a low dielectric constant and are frequently used to prevent objects from coming into contact with one another. However, achieving high dielectric constants in plastic materials remains challenging \[[83](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_083)\]. Several recent initiatives have employed data-driven approaches to develop high dielectric polymers.
    
    ### 11.7.3 Polymer membrane design for gas separation
    
    Polymers are also excellent choices for gas separation due to their enormous surface area \[84\]. Since the early 1990s, people have been particularly interested in a class of polymers known as polymers of intrinsic microporosity \[84\]. Researchers must investigate the creation of new polymeric membranes because the existing ones have poor selectivity and degrade over time \[[85](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_085)\]. It’s not easy, though, to come up with polymer membranes that work well and let a lot of gas through while also being selective. Some early research has been conducted to accelerate the search for polymer membranes using data-driven methodologies. For example, gas permeability prediction models have been developed, and the enumeration approach has been utilized to identify polymer membrane candidates for separating CO[2] and CH[4] \[[86](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_086)\].
    
    ### 11.7.4 Inverse design of thermally conductive polymers
    
    Due to their versatility and ease of manipulation, polymers are increasingly being used as materials for semiconductors, energy storage devices, and several micro/nano fluidics devices. The long-term stability, sustainability, and durability of these devices depend on their ability to effectively dissipate heat. This is because they generate significant heat during operation. The naturally low heat conductivity of polymers needs to be raised so that they can be used successfully in the above-mentioned situations \[[87](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_087)\]. To comprehend and control the thermal conductivity of polymeric materials, a great deal of research has been conducted. These studies demonstrate that polymer conductivity is intimately related to how they are structured, what chemicals they contain, how they interact with other chemicals, and a variety of other environmental conditions and industrial conditions \[[88](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_088)\]. These intricate relationships offer thermally conductive polymers a wide range of design options.
    
    ### 11.7.5 Conducting polymer design for electronic applications
    
    Polymers usually don’t conduct electricity, but some of them do. These intrinsically conducting polymers are used in electronics such as field-effect transistors, light-emitting diodes, and organic solar cells \[[89](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_089)\]. Molecular doping is often used to make polymers even more conductive, but it takes longer to find the best pairs of polymers and dopants that work well together. This is because the working conditions, how the dopants and polymers interact, and how the electrons move are all very complicated \[[90](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_090)\]. Polymer informatics can improve this process by developing models that predict conductivity and utilizing iterative methods to identify the best polymer-dopant pairs. It is supported by the fact that random forest and enhanced regression trees were used to find many good donor/acceptor pairs for organic solar cells \[[91](#chapter-011.xhtml#b_9783111681870-011_ref_091)\].
    
    ## 11.8 Future research directions
    
    The promise of artificial intelligence and ML in polymer science is not without its obstacles, which must be overcome before the field can fully benefit from these technologies.
    
    ### 11.8.1 Data quality and quantity
    
    Dataset growth and improvement should be the researchers’ priority. This method allows for the collection of a vast amount of high-resolution experimental data, which significantly improves model training and validation.
    
    ### 11.8.2 Algorithm development
    
    It is important to keep coming up with new methods and techniques, especially for dealing with problems that keep coming up, like overfitting, generalization, and processing efficiency. ML techniques that are mixed in hybrid models may also be a good way to boost speed.
    
    ### 11.8.3 Computational resources
    
    Training and using cutting-edge ML models require a lot of work.
    
    ## 11.9 Conclusion
    
    In conclusion, the combination of AI and ML with polymer science has opened up fresh opportunities for material exploration. Researchers can use ML algorithms to quickly screen and optimize polymer qualities, accelerating the development of new materials. AI can predict the behavior of polymers at various stages, including monomer selection, polymerization, and the polymer’s final properties. This enables the development of polymers with customized characteristics for specific purposes.
    
    The combination of polymers and AI has far-reaching implications for a variety of areas. For example, the design of polymer membranes for gas separation, polymer electrolytes for lithium-ion batteries, and rational polymer dielectrics. Furthermore, AI can help create polymers for energy storage devices such as super capacitors and batteries. We may expect the development of breakthrough polymer-based goods that will improve many aspects of our lives as long as research in this area continues. Finally, the combination of AI and polymers has the potential to transform material science and other domains.
