These agents can be encapsulated by smart polymers, which shield them from early deterioration and guarantee their stability until release \[[17](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_017)\]. Patient adherence to treatment plans is enhanced by smart polymer-based DDS, which decreases the frequency of medication administration and permits noninvasive delivery methods. Injectable gels with continuous release, for instance, can replace daily injections, improving patient compliance and comfort \[[18](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_018)\].
    
    Notwithstanding the encouraging benefits, there are still several obstacles to overcome in the creation and use of smart polymers in medication delivery. For clinical use, it is essential that smart polymers are biocompatible and nontoxic. To evaluate these materials’ long-term impact on the body, thorough research is needed \[[15](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_015)\]. Large-scale production may be hampered by the intricacy of creating smart polymers. For them to be widely used, manufacturing procedures must be developed that are both affordable and repeatable \[[17](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_017)\]. It can take a long time and a lot of resources to navigate the regulatory environment for novel compounds, which calls for extensive safety and effectiveness documentation \[[17](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_017)\].
    
    ### 13.2.2 Case study
    
    This study aims to advance the field of materials science with specific applications in biomedicine, focusing on the development of innovative DDS. The research sought to engineer novel “smart” materials, particularly thermoresponsive polymers like poly(*N*\-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM), which exhibit LCSTs near physiological levels (~32 °C). Such materials are of significant interest for applications in tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, and controlled drug delivery due to their ability to undergo reversible phase transitions in response to thermal stimuli.
    
    The study introduced an innovative approach utilizing the magnetocaloric effect (MCE) of FeRh alloys to noninvasively modulate the properties of PNIPAM. Unlike conventional heating methods that rely on intrusive components or direct thermal inputs, this technique leverages external magnetic fields to trigger phase transitions. FeRh alloys were selected for their exceptional MCE performance near physiological temperatures and reduced cytotoxicity compared to traditional materials like gadolinium (Gd). The overarching objective was to address the challenges of developing biocompatible, magnetically triggered drug-release systems that are clinically viable.
    
    A novel PNIPAM/FeRh composite material was engineered to explore magnetically controlled drug delivery mechanisms. The composite was fabricated using PNIPAM polymer, Fe49Rh51 alloy, and the chemotherapeutic agent doxorubicin (DOX), with ethanol as the solvent. The FeRh alloy substrate was prepared via arc melting high-purity Fe and Rh powders, followed by annealing at 1,000 °C and rapid quenching. PNIPAM was deposited onto the FeRh substrate through solvent-casting, forming a polymer layer approximately 20 µm thick. To enhance drug-loading efficiency and adhesion, laser-engraved microwells were created on the FeRh surface. These wells were subsequently filled with DOX and overlaid with a PNIPAM coating, serving as reservoirs for drug storage and enabling controlled release.
    
    The composite demonstrated temperature-responsive behavior at the LCST of PNIPAM (32 °C), driven by MCEs induced by a 3 T magnetic field – parameters compatible with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems. Advanced optical imaging and spectroscopic analyses, including UV-VIS and Raman spectroscopy, validated the controlled release of DOX. The biocompatibility of the PNIPAM/FeRh scaffold was evaluated using mouse embryonic fibroblasts, which exhibited effective adhesion, spreading, and proliferation over 72 h. Cells were observed to localize both on the polymer’s surface and within the laser-engraved wells, underscoring the material’s cytocompatibility.
    
    These findings underscore the potential of the PNIPAM/FeRh composite for developing magnetically activated DDSs and advanced biomedical implants \[[19](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_019)\].
    
    ## 13.3 AI-driven predictive modeling
    
    Predictive modeling in materials science, is the use of computational techniques, particularly ML. AI is employed to predict the properties of materials based on their structural and compositional data. It is critical for rational design strategies to improve the understanding of the properties of materials and biomacromolecules. To increase efficacy and minimize adverse effects, by simulating and predicting the behavior of drug delivery devices, we can utilize sophisticated computational approaches. Characteristics like droplet size and drug loading efficiency in self-microemulsifying DDSs (SMEDDSs) have been optimized using ML methods such as linear regression. By analyzing intricate relationships between formulation elements, these models can produce drug delivery methods that are more successful \[[20](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_020)\].
    
    Customized therapy regimens that adapt to each patient’s specific physiological circumstances are created through integration with real-time data and medical imaging. When combined with in vitro characterization, in silico modeling provides a reliable framework for predicting DDS formulation performance in vivo, thereby reducing the need for animal testing. By enhancing understanding of how formulations behave in human physiology, this approach improves treatment outcomes \[[21](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_021)\].
    
    ### 13.3.1 Machine learning techniques in predictive modeling
    
    In ML, the focus is on making an accurate prediction, or the “what,” rather than the “how.” For instance, in image recognition for cancer diagnosis, the relationship between the individual features (pixels) and the result is relatively irrelevant if the prediction is accurate. Algorithms are mathematical procedures that describe the relationships between variables \[[22](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_022)\]. They are of two types:
    
    1.  Easily interpretable, that is, Auditable Algorithms
        
    2.  Not easily interpretable, that is, black boxes.
        
    
    A comparison between Auditable Algorithms and Black Boxes is given in the [table 13.1](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_tab_001).
    
    Table 13.1:Comparison between auditable algorithms and black boxes \[[23](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_023)\].
    
    | Auditable algorithms || Black boxes |
    | --- | --- |
    | Simple models, better for interpretation. || Complex models, better for complex data. |
    | --- | --- |
    | Includes multiple regression and decision trees. || Includes neural networks and certain support vector machines. |
    | Can be used on consumer PCs, so they are computationally cheap. || Computationally expensive, as they require an increase in processor time to build models. |
    | Interpretation is easier due to the linear relationship between predictors and outcomes. || Nonlinear relationships make interpretation difficult. |
    | More like statistical techniques. || Few commonalities exist with statistical techniques. |
    
    Most ML techniques fall into one of two categories: supervised and unsupervised.
    
    #### 13.3.1.1 Supervised learning
    
    In supervised ML, a model is trained for a variety of input ranges, also known as features, and an association is made on the basis of the outcome. It establishes a relationship between independent and dependent variables. For example, relating the weight and smoking status of a person to greater chances of getting diabetes. After training the algorithm, the model can predict the outcome in new data as well.
    
    There are different types of predictions made by supervised learning (SL) models, including:
    
    1.  **Continuous**, offering a range, for example, a number from 0 to 100. Also called a regression algorithm \[[24](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_024)\], as it relates to the prediction of continuous values. Regression algorithm in ML predicts a dose for chemotherapy that is tolerable or can be used to predict an individual’s life expectancy.
        
    2.  **Discrete** classifies the output in a yes-or-no format, for example, positive or negative results; cancer is either benign or malignant, based on which the diagnosis is predicted. It is also referred to as a classification algorithm.
        
    
    ![Figure 13.1: Flowchart of supervised learning algorithm training and output prediction.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-013_fig_001.jpg)
    
    Figure 13.1: Flowchart of supervised learning algorithm training and output prediction.
    
    SL has some limitations, such as the input data used to train the algorithm might not fit well with new data. However, this risk of overfitting can be eradicated by employing various techniques. For example, splitting a dataset into training and testing datasets. This randomization allows the algorithm to associate the characteristics with outcomes, and as a result, the algorithm also generalizes well to new datasets \[[23](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_023)\].
    
    A flow chart showing steps involved in output prediction by supervised learning is shown in [figure 13.1](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_fig_001).
    
    #### 13.3.1.2 Unsupervised learning
    
    Unsupervised learning, as the name implies, does not require supervision; that is, user input data is not necessary. There is no predetermined result; instead, patterns are created by algorithms. As a result, this method is exploratory and aids in identifying unknown patterns or clusters in the dataset.
    
    Because they are often used to decrease the number of features or dimensions in the analysis, unsupervised learning techniques are also known as **dimension reduction techniques**. The algorithm receives raw data and clusters it into a collection of related data points. The algorithm excludes data if it is insufficient for grouping. The workflow for unsupervised learning is represented in [figure 13.2](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_fig_002). Principal component analysis (PCA), t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE), and latent Dirichlet analysis are the procedures used in these methods \[[25](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_025)\].
    
    ![Figure 13.2: Workflow of unsupervised learning.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-013_fig_002.jpg)
    
    Figure 13.2: Workflow of unsupervised learning.
    
    Supervised and unsupervised learning techniques are further classified into three fundamental ML techniques.
    
    1.  **Linear regression**: An algorithm for SL. A linear relationship is established by fitting the data along a line between the features (an independent variable) and the target (a dependent variable) \[[26](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_026)\].
        
    2.  **K means clustering:** An algorithm for unsupervised learning. The main objective is to find groups in the data that are represented by the variable K. K applied to unlabeled data.
        
    3.  **Decision trees**: Hierarchical structure algorithm for nonparametric SL that may be applied to both regression and classification problems.
        
    
    It includes key components such as the **root node** (representing the entire dataset), **decision nodes** (where splits occur), **branches** (connecting nodes), and **leaf nodes** (final outcomes).
    
    The tree-building process involves splitting the dataset into subsets and reducing, to enhance performance and prevent overfitting. Each path from the root to a leaf represents a unique decision rule. Decision trees are appreciated for their simplicity, effectiveness, and interpretability in decision-making \[[27](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_027)\]. A simple structure of decision tree is represented in [figure 13.3](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_fig_003).
    
    ![Figure 13.3: Basic structure of decision trees.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-013_fig_003.jpg)
    
    Figure 13.3: Basic structure of decision trees.
    
    ### 13.3.2 Supervised algorithms for multiple inputs dataset
    
    Other supervised ML techniques for multi-input datasets include:
    
    #### 13.3.2.1 Logistic regression
    
    These are close to multivariate logistic regression. It involves the utilization of regularization functions that reduce the magnitudes of features. A study demonstrated the use of logistic regression in identifying prostate cancer. The technique employed was, desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometric imaging of small metabolites and lipids.
    
    #### 13.3.2.2 Support vector machine
    
    Provide accurate predictions for scenarios when there is a nonlinear relationship between features and the outcomes. It employs a kernel trick model that separates two groups by hyperplane or a decision boundary \[[28](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_028)\].
    
    **Artificial neural network (ANNs):**  ANNs have a complex architecture because these are somewhat modeled on the neuronal structure of the mammalian cortex. These networks make it possible to combine the study of artificial intelligence and biology, and they offer a rich environment for simulating human memory and learning \[[29](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_029)\]. Recurrent and convolutional networks are examples of specialty neural networks that have been added to ANNs and have produced remarkable results on a variety of tasks. ANNs are prone to over-fitting due to their highly parameterized designs. They can perform better if regularization techniques are used \[[23](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_023)\]. [Figure 13.4](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_fig_004) illustrates the integration of Graph Neural Networks and Multitask Learning as ‘Fast’ and ‘Accurate’ respectively.
    
    ![Figure 13.4: Graph neural net and multitask learning.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-013_fig_004.jpg)
    
    Figure 13.4: Graph neural net and multitask learning.
    
    ### 13.3.3 Neural networks and deep learning
    
    Neural networks are built with several neurons that reflect the information extracted from each feature in the dataset. As information goes between ‘neurons’ or nodes, it is multiplied by the neuron’s weight and changed by an activation function.
    
    #### 13.3.3.1 Deep neural networks (DNNs)
    
    Deep neural networks (DNNs) have many hidden layers. The term “deep” in DNNs refers to the depth of the network, which is determined by the number of hidden layers. Usually, it contains three hidden layers. Deep learning utilizes DNNs and produces impressive results when used for complex tasks, such as image recognition and computer-assisted diagnosis of melanoma. Deeper networks require additional weights and biases to be optimized during training because of the growing number of connections between nodes. The successful training of DNNs has been made possible by improvements in hardware and optimization methods, even though this may present difficulties in terms of computing complexity and training time \[[31](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_031)\].
    
    #### 13.3.3.2 Convolutional neural network (CNN)
    
    Convolutional neural network (CNN) is a deep learning approach that has been widely used in computer vision tasks, including picture categorization and object recognition.
    
    Despite its impressive achievements, deep learning still has limitations when compared to human intelligence \[[29](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_029)\]. Complex techniques are required to improve model performance and interpretability in the face of issues like overfitting and vanishing gradients.
    
    An analysis on various ML algorithms for ML model development is provided in [table 13.2](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_tab_002). Lower MSE and higher *R*² indicate better model performance \[[32](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_032)\].
    
    Table 13.2:Properties of machine learning algorithms \[[32](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_032)\].
    
    | Algorithm || Size of dataset || Mean squared error (MSE) || *R²* || Avg prediction time |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | ANNs || 1,000 || 1.89 || 0.92 || 0.015 |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | SVM || 800 || 2.15 || 0.88 || 0.010 |
    | Decision trees || 600 || 2.50 || 0.82 || 0.003 |
    
    ### 13.3.4 Deep learning in polymer behavior prediction and drug delivery
    
    Drug-phospholipid complexing is a formulation approach used to enhance the bioavailability of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). However, predicting the candidacy of lipidic drug candidates in in-vitro experiments is a time-consuming and not very cost-effective technique. A study predicted the production of drug-phospholipid complexes using ML algorithms. However, the decrease in test performance caused by the small size of the training data was not adequately addressed.
    
    In 2023, Yoo et al. \[33\] presented a novel deep learning-based prediction algorithm to address this issue. In order to improve prediction performance, it used PCA and variational autoencoder (VAE) approaches. And to accurately depict the intricate link between medications and lipid molecules, the model makes use of a multilayer one-dimensional CNN with a skip connection. With a high sensitivity of 97.5%, the suggested model was able to identify interesting candidate medications, underscoring the need of creating effective prediction models \[[33](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_033)\].
    
    The efficacy of ML in handling intricate predictive tasks pertaining to polymer behavior and drug delivery in pharmaceutical formulations is demonstrated by another study, which shows that different neural network architectures can precisely predict drug release profiles from polymer-based long-acting injectables \[[34](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_034)\].
    
    ## 13.4 Virtual screening techniques
    
    Virtual screening techniques (VSTs) involve the use of computational tools and approaches to screen a large compound library to identify and predict the biological activity and affinity of a drug molecule for a specific target \[[24](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_024)\].
    
    The history of computer-aided drug design dates back to the 1950s, when computational approaches were first used to generate NMR simulations, marking the initial steps in the field’s evolution. Multiple modeling tools were used to solve complex regression equations; however, the intricate spatial structure of molecules limited the scope of structural activity relationships. In the 1970s, graphical programs representing HOMO, LUMO, and bipolar moments of molecules were developed. These advancements overcame the barriers associated with in silico prediction of molecular properties with their theoretical results. Similarly, powerful genetic and biochemical screening tools for the prediction of desired active compounds from various extracts have been developed in recent decades \[[24](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_024), [35](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_035)\].
    
    AI-driven virtual screening expedites the discovery of novel two-dimensional materials with tailored physical and chemical properties, offering significant potential for energy conversion and storage applications. ML-assisted virtual screening facilitates the identification of promising low-potential candidate molecules for organic redox-active polymers in battery applications. The incorporation of information technology has revolutionized drug discovery, empowering researchers to efficiently screen extensive compound libraries and make precise predictions about their biological functions \[[36](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_036)\].
    
    ### 13.4.1 AI algorithms in virtual screening
    
    ML, deep learning, and other computer techniques are used by AI-based virtual displays to evaluate pharmacological parameters and biological data. Artificial intelligence is defined as a superset of ML, which includes supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning (RL). Furthermore, deep learning, a subset of ML, is widely used in drug research and development. The algorithms used in drug design and discovery include ANNs, deep neural networks, support vector machines, classification and regression, generative adversarial networks (GANs), symbolic learning, and meta-learning.
    
    A few of the drug discovery processes that have used these algorithms are structure and ligand-based virtual screening, toxicity prediction, drug monitoring and release, pharmacophore modeling, and quantitative structure–activity relationship, etc. Furthermore, newly created modeling algorithms were crucially supported by innovative data mining, curation, and management strategies \[[37](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_037)\].
    
    #### 13.4.1.1 Genetic algorithms
    
    Genetic algorithms, a nature-mimicking optimization method, are stochastic global optimization approaches based on evolutionary biology. This concept is analogous to the genotype-phenotype relationship in evolutionary biology, which relates to the chemical issue of comprehending the structure-property relationship. Together with theoretical techniques like force-fields and high-throughput first-principles methods, GA has been widely applied in chemistry and materials science. Consequently, the approach enables precise and automated structure determination.
    
    Plane‒cut‒splice (PCS) crossover, rattle mutation (ratt.), and permutation mutation (perm.) are some of the operators implemented in GAMaterial for atomic clusters and interfaces \[[38](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_038)\].
    
    #### 13.4.1.2 GA algorithm in polymer design
    
    The GA algorithm can help with polymer design by quickly and consistently producing novel polymer candidates for specified applications. It can be used to generate polymer candidates depending on user-defined properties like glass transition temperature (*T*[g]) and bandgap \[[39](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_039)\]. The GA algorithm uses crossover and mutation operations to change the sequence of chemical building blocks in polymers and generate new progeny. The fitness of the offspring is assessed using ML models, which yield rapid property estimations. Only the best-performing kids are kept as parent polymers, and the procedure is repeated until sufficient polymer candidates with the requisite qualities are discovered \[[36](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_036)\].
    
    #### 13.4.1.3 Genetic algorithm software and polymer development
    
    To clarify the architectures of atomic clusters, doped clusters or materials, and atomic clusters on surfaces, Lourenço et al. offer a new genetic algorithm program called GAMaterial, which is written in Python3.x and conducts global searches.
    
    The following is the workflow for GAMaterial’s implementation of the genetic algorithm method for automatic polymer discovery and development:
    
    1.  **Initial structure generation:** DFT (density functional theory) or DFTB(density-functional tight binding) methods are used to build a set of random polymer structures, which are then locally optimized.
        
    2.  **Progenitor structure selection**: After the population has been established, progenitor polymer structures are chosen based on a proportion of the lowest-energy configurations.
        
    3.  **Crossover and mutation:** The selected progenitors are permitted to undergo crossover and/or mutation to produce offspring polymer structures. To assure dissimilarity between offspring structures and current structures, a filter operator can be utilized based on parameters such as relative cumulative difference between polymer isomers and maximum interatomic distance difference.
        
    4.  **Random selection and ML integration**: Next, a subset of structures is randomly chosen from the newly formed progeny. Alternatively, a ML regression model can be applied to the offspring structures to forecast total energies, allowing for the selection of the most promising structures to generate the next population following local optimization.
        
    5.  **Local optimization and iteration:** The chosen structures are then locally optimized. An elitist option can be used to ensure that the next population always has the lowest-energy local minimum structure \[[38](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_038)\]. A simple workflow for GA Material in polymer discovery is shown in [figure 13.5](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_fig_005).
        
    
    ![Figure 13.5: Workflow for GAMaterial in polymer discovery.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-013_fig_005.jpg)
    
    Figure 13.5: Workflow for GAMaterial in polymer discovery.
    
    ### 13.4.2 Reinforcement learning in polymerization control
    
    RL is a subfield of ML in which machines gradually learn control behaviors through self-exploration of their surroundings. Deep RL (DRL) is a versatile solution to control problems. The fundamental advantage of the RL algorithm is that it learns to optimize control policies by exploring the environment, regardless of the system’s linearity or multivariability.
    
    Polymerization reactions are difficult to control because the product quality and various polymeric architectures are dictated by molecular mass distribution (MMD). DRL approaches, such as deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), can handle continuous control activities, such as altering monomer and initiator flow rates in real time. The controller learns from historical data and adapts its tactics in response to performance feedback, allowing it to efficiently deal with polymerization process fluctuations \[[40](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_040)\].
    
    ### 13.4.3 Smart polymer screening
    
    Smart polymer screening is utilized to identify and optimize polymer formulations rapidly by predicting their properties using advanced computational techniques, including RL. Similar to its role in polymerization control, RL can adaptively refine screening processes based on real-time feedback regarding polymer characteristics.
    
    Repeating units of polymers act as chemo-structural entities that help in the screening of polymers from libraries of candidate polymers. ML exploits this feature, that is, the polymer repeat unit, for extraction and screening. Few approaches utilized for this purpose are neural networks, multitask learning,, and other deep learning techniques.
    
    Neural network is one of the approaches utilized in ML for natural language processing. In this technique, material is represented either in the form of a simplified molecular input line entry system (SMILES) or as graphs.
    
    The main concept of multitask learning involves training a model to learn various target properties simultaneously. Hence, the risk of overfitting one target property is ruled out and overall performance is improved \[[30](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_030)\].
    
    ### 13.4.4 Case study: screening of polymeric-nanoparticle system for treatment of cancer
    
    Inadequate loading and premature drug release are the key limitations of drug delivery by nanoparticles for tumors. Both properties are essential for cancer treatment. To combat cytotoxicity, nanoparticles are exploited for targeted drug delivery; however, reduced retention time poses toxicity threats.
    
    A study conducted by Animasawun and his colleagues in 2020 employed reverse engineering techniques. They investigated drug‒polymer interactions between etoposide, etoposide phosphate, and teniposide, as well as nine polymers: PGA, PGA–PEG, PGA40%C8, PGA40%C18, PGA85%C18, PGA30%CH, PGA50%TRY, PGA50%Phe, and PGA50%SA. Polymers employed for nanoparticle preparation were PGA50%TRY for teniposide and PGA85%C18 for etoposide and etoposide phosphate. The drug loading obtained from the nanoprecipitation technique was 13% for teniposide, 5% for etoposide, and less than 5% for etoposide phosphate.
    
    The study demonstrated that the selection of polymers for each drug produced nanoparticles with improved properties. For screening, three different approaches were employed, including high-throughput drug release experiments, FTIR spectroscopy, and contact angle measurements. Contact angle measurements and FTIR explained the results of drug release using solid dispersion films. [Table 13.3](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_tab_003) provides the percentage of drug released in 24h for different drug-polymer films and drug-loaded nanoparticles. The major factor that affected the drug release behavior of polymers was the polymer‒drug interaction. This interaction resulted in peak shifts due to side-chain rearrangement.
    
    Table 13.3:Percentage of drug released in 24 h (drug–polymer films and drug-loaded nanoparticles) \[[41](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_041)\].
    
    | System || % drug released in 24 h |
    | --- | --- |
    | Teniposide–PGA50%TRY film || 29 |
    | --- | --- |
    | Teniposide–PGA50%TRY nanoparticles || 35 |
    | Etoposide–PGA85%C18 film || 64 |
    | Etoposide–PGA85%C18 nanoparticles || 22 |
    | Etoposide phosphate–PGA85%C18 film || 23.8 |
    | Etoposide phosphate–PGA85%C18 nanoparticles || 16 |
    
    #### 13.4.4.1 Results
    
    The three polymer‒drug combinations employed in this study demonstrated that the formulation with the best drug loading had the poorest drug retention, whereas the formulation with the lowest drug loading had the best drug retention. This study showed that drug‒polymer interactions should be considered when creating polymer nanoparticle formulations. In conclusion, screening for polymer interactions can help in choosing the right polymer-drug matches to increase drug loading and lower drug release rates \[[41](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_041)\].
    
    ### 13.4.5 Case study: computational technique for enhancing transdermal delivery of peptides
    
    Skin-penetrating peptides (SPPs) are becoming increasingly popular as a non-invasive method of transdermal medication delivery. However, it is time-consuming to identify SPP sequences through experimental screening of peptide libraries. According to recent research, SPPs need to exhibit an affinity for both the medication of interest and skin keratin to function as effective enhancers.
    
    To find SPPs that could improve transdermal CsA delivery, Menegatti and colleagues in 2016 developed a computational procedure. They created and screened virtual libraries of disulfide-cyclic peptides against keratin and cyclosporine A (CsA). The chosen sequences were evaluated experimentally and were found to bind both CsA and keratin and enhance transdermal permeation of CsA. This was determined by mass spectrometry and affinity chromatography. Four heptameric sequences stood out as top candidates. An octameric peptide produced noticeably higher delivery of CsA than heptameric SPPs. Incubation with skin keratinocytes further confirmed the chosen sequences’ safety profile. This approach proved to be efficient for delivering the required ingredients for medicinal and cosmeceutical purposes \[[39](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_039)\].
    
    ## 13.5 Advanced characterization of nanomaterials
    
    Nanotechnology represents a seminal technological advancement of the twenty-first century. Nanoparticles find applications across diverse domains such as medicine, materials science, agriculture, and environmental engineering, facilitating the achievement of substantial outcomes within these disciplines. Notwithstanding the considerable progress in this technological sphere, a substantial disparity in the understanding of the surfaces of these nanoparticles persists. As a result, defining these particles is essential for shedding light on their traits, functions, and impacts. The most critical attributes encompass dimensions, morphology, elemental composition, and surface charge density, among others.
    
    Various strategies are applied in pursuit of this aim, highlighting the importance of spectroscopic, microscopic, and zetapotential  assessments of the nanoparticles. The primary aim is to formulate an appropriate dosage form that maximizes the potential benefits derived from these particles \[[42](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_042)\].
    
    Nanomaterials exhibit interactions with biological macromolecules. The degree of such interactions is contingent upon the physicochemical characteristics of these nanoparticles. These interactions exert a considerable influence on the efficacy of targeted delivery, bioimaging, and diagnostic applications, all contributing to favorable outcomes. Nonetheless, the surface charge of nanoparticles can induce conformational alterations or perturbations in membranes or proteins, which are generally deemed unfavorable. As the discipline of nanomaterial synthesis transitions from a predominantly empirical approach to a more predictable framework, it becomes feasible to achieve anisotropic growth across various facets when the capping ligand selectively engages with a specific facet of the nanocrystal, thereby facilitating shape control during nanoparticle synthesis.
    
    This advancement is facilitated by the capacity to characterize the capping ligands and monitor the surface composition of the nanoparticles, which is essential for elucidating the roles of ligands in the modulation of nanoparticle growth \[[43](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_043)\]. As a result, enhanced characterization of nanomaterials helps establish structure‒property relationships and also aids in the generation of design recommendations, boosting the benefit‒risk ratio \[[44](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_044)\].
    
    ### 13.5.1 AI-enhanced techniques for characterization
    
    By leveraging advanced algorithms, one can enhance the accuracy and efficiency of techniques for the characterization of nanomaterials. Various methodologies are employed for increasing the comprehension of nanomaterial applications, which are described further.
    
    #### 13.5.1.1 Image processing
    
    AI-enhanced techniques for nanomaterial characterization include generative models, graph neural networks, transfer learning, adversarial training, attention mechanisms, and federated learning.
    
    Generative models and graph neural networks are used for image processing techniques such as **scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM****), X-ray diffraction, and atomic force microscopy** \[[45](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_045)\].
    
    Deep learning algorithms are based on neural networks that provide real-time identification and characterization of 2D materials. These extract complex graphical features from imaging data to predict physical properties effectively. Recently, denoising frameworks that need no supervision have been developed. These algorithms enhance the clarity of nanoparticle surface dynamics. And the time for resolution through electron microscopy for atomic resolution observations of nanomaterials, is decreased down to 10 ms. This allows better surface characterization \[[46](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_046)\].
    
    #### 13.5.1.2 Optimization of nanomaterial synthesis
    
    High-throughput screening (HTS) is one of the traditional methods for the screening of candidate drugs. Newer AI optimization methods are shown to outperform these traditional techniques by enhancing chemical material discovery, efficiency, and precision. They are utilized in nanocrystal synthesis, producing better-quality products with limited resource utilization and less carbon emissions \[[47](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_047)\].
    
    #### 13.5.1.3 Toxicological assessment
    
    The identification of critical parameters for assessing the safety of nanomaterials is facilitated by ML techniques. Decision tree algorithms are employed to analyze and compare datasets, along with the integration of text and data mining in nanotoxicology. Some frameworks, such as ISA-TAB Nano, are utilized for systemic data collection. It facilitates insights into structure‒toxicity relationships and predictive modeling \[[48](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_048)\].
    
    ### 13.5.2 Application of AI in spectroscopy, microscopy, and rheology of smart polymers and nanomaterials
    
    AI algorithms facilitate the design and simulation of smart polymers, such as LCST polymers with diverse stimulus responses, optimizing their properties and biodegradability for biomedical applications \[[49](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_049)\]. ML methods can predict the behavior of shape memory polymers (SMPs). The approach to describe SMPs combines video data analysis and predictive modeling. As a result, we can achieve greater accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity in predicting their behavior \[[50](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_050)\].
    
    #### 13.5.2.1 AI-assisted spectroscopy
    
    Artificial intelligence, particularly neural networks, improves the accuracy and efficiency of spectral interpretation. Studies have shown that  ANNs may efficiently measure polymer-based cocrystal formulations using Raman and FTIR spectroscopy. By reaching low root mean square error (RMSE) values, these indicate strong predictive accuracy. In 2018, Barmpalexis et al. investigated the presence of carbamazepine‒nicotinamide (CBZ/NIC) and ibuprofen‒nicotinamide (IBU/NIC) cocrystals in Soluplus® formulations. Raman and attenuated total reflectance Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) were employed for this purpose.
    
    The spectrum peaks were demonstrated using feed-forward, back-propagation  ANNs, and partial least squares regression analysis. They concluded that incorporating AI-based model techniques into FTIR and Raman studies increased the root mean squared error of prediction (RMSEp) \[[51](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_051)\].
    
    AI is used in massively parallel spectroscopy (MPS), which allows the observation of bio conjugated nanoparticles. MPS analyzes complicated biological matrices without increasing background noise, making it useful in real-world applications with a detection limit of 1.6 fmol/L.. ML models have been developed to predict the mechanical performance of polymer nanocomposites reinforced with silver-coated gold nanoparticles (AgC NPs) using tensile test data, indicating ideal compositions for enhanced characteristics \[[52](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_052)\].
    
    #### 13.5.2.2 AI in microscopy of smart polymers and nanomaterials
    
    It is challenging to characterize the surface dynamics of nanoparticles at atomic precision since it requires high temporal and spatial resolution. Traditional ultrafast TEM has a nanoscale spatial resolution limit, despite its ability to achieve picosecond temporal resolution. AI-driven unsupervised denoising frameworks allow for clearer visualization of metal nanoparticle surfaces in TEM. This improves spatiotemporal characterization, achieving time resolutions down to 10 ms while minimizing noise and electron damage. This advancement aids in understanding atomic-level structural dynamics in materials and regulating diffusion, reactivity, and catalysis functionalities \[[46](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_046)\].
    
    Researchers can effectively visualize nanoscale morphologies by converting SEM pictures into feature representations using a deep learning-based approach \[[53](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_053)\]. In order to improve nanoparticle categorization and segmentation, GANs produce synthetic SEM images that may be used. These are employed to train  CNNs, expanding the amount of training data available for deep learning models \[[54](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_054)\]. AI pipelines enhance the identification and classification of DNA molecules under electron microscopy (EM). These specifically employ gold nanoparticle-tagged peptides for visualization, highlighting the potential for AI in biological applications of microscopy \[[55](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_055)\].
    
    #### 13.5.2.3 AI in rheology for material behavior prediction
    
    The storage and loss moduli of 3D-printed polyacrylamide hydrogels have been successfully predicted using deep learning models, such as multilayer perceptrons, which achieve an R² value of 0.89. This makes it possible to accurately map material behavior from a small number of input factors \[[56](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_056)\]. The dynamic behavior of magnetorheological elastomers in tension-compression modes is predicted using ANNs. With *R*² values above 0.97, this demonstrates how well ANNs can represent intricate nonlinear interactions between input parameters and material stress \[[75](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_075)\].
    
    ### 13.5.3 Integration of AI for data analysis in polymer nanocomposites
    
    The organic matrix materials, known as polymer nanocomposites, contain nanoparticles with at least one dimension smaller than 100 nm \[[57](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_057)\]. To forecast the characteristics of nanocomposite materials, researchers have developed various numerical techniques, such as multiscale simulations and continuum mechanical approaches \[[58](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_058)\].
    
    An open-source, data-driven, web-based platform called NanoMine has been created in the field of nanocomposite technology. Composition, processing techniques, microstructural pictures, and measurable properties are among the experimental and computational data on nanocomposites that are archived \[[59](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_059)\].
    
    Wang et al. performed an experiment demonstrating the integration of deep learning to predict the mechanical properties of nanocomposites. The results demonstrated that the suggested deep learning model increases the accuracy of predicting the rubbery modulus by **34.2%**, the glass modulus by **45.2%**, and the tan δ peak by **19.7%** \[[60](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_060)\].
    
    ### 13.5.4 AI tools providing deeper insights
    
    Drug development is being greatly improved by AI tools, which offer deeper insights through sophisticated methods such as PCA and clustering.
    
    These are ML techniques that are employed to classify polymer morphologies, aiding in the design of multicomponent systems for applications like drug delivery. By reducing dimensionality in large datasets, the PCA technique makes it possible to visualize and comprehend molecular interactions and therapeutic efficacy more clearly. AI identifies biomarkers, therapeutic targets, and integrates multi-omics data \[[61](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_061)\].
    
    Similar biological data can be grouped by AI algorithms using the clustering technique, which helps identify targets related to diseases and possible treatment candidates.
    
    ### 13.5.6 Case study: AI-aided polymeric structure optimization for enhanced gene delivery
    
    ![Figure 13.6: Schematic illustration of PCD prediction by XGBoost.](graphic/converted/b_9783111681870-013_fig_006.jpg)
    
    Figure 13.6: Schematic illustration of PCD prediction by XGBoost.
    
    Development of gene therapy vectors, especially polymeric vectors, has always been a challenge due to a lack of understanding of their internal structure. A study by Li et al. in 2023 investigated the impact of polymeric structure on gene transfection efficiency. They utilized a well-known polymeric vector, poly(β-amino ester) (PAE), for experimentation. AI was employed to understand the relationship between polymer component distribution (PCD) and gene delivery. The study examined the characteristics of individual polymeric components and their combinations to understand how they exert synergistic effects on gene delivery.
    
    #### 13.5.6.1 Results
    
    The effect of PCD on transfection performance was investigated, and AI was incorporated. PCD prediction by XG Boost is illustrated in [figure 13.6](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_fig_006). AI adjusted the PCDs, targeting high transfection efficiency, and further optimized the composition of polymers. A library of polymers (9 × 10⁵) with different PCDs was computer-generated. Next, a trained AI XGBoost model was employed to identify the optimal polymers and evaluate the transfection efficiency. In vitro experiments validated the predictions made by AI. In vitro analysis showed that the transfection efficiency of the PAE-B1-based polyplex was roughly 1.5 times that of Lipo3000 and 2 times that of jetPEI. This analysis served as the basis for the development of several highly effective polymer vectors \[[62](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_062)\].
    
    ## 13.6 Challenges and limitations
    
    Despite having several advantages over the typical ways of DDS design, AI-integrated drug designing faces some shortcomings and practical challenges limiting its further usage, and using modern AI technology for better research. In this part of the chapter, we will have a deep insight into the current limitations in AI integration with DDS, and we will consider how AI-aided predictive modeling and VSTs are currently facing real-world setbacks. Furthermore, the ethical parameters and considerations accounted for AI applications will also be discussed.
    
    ### 13.6.1 Data quality and accuracy
    
    The fundamentals of AI-integrated designing are the availability and access to accurate and reliable datasets with up-to-date, valid information accessible to researchers, as well as the availability of reliable resources that are detailed for best results.
    
    The basic consideration to be focused on in developing DDS designs using AI and the future innovation of DDS is the lack of availability of current literature with modern narratives and the variation in current available datasets, which lack transparency in the available literature. Literature is available in the form of datasets, statistical sets, or raw unstructured information, which is being integrated by modern AI tools. These data arrays make all the necessary information and knowledge needed for the future advancement and successful implementation of any new or older research and practical implementation of ideas being executed for the most reliable results and in this case (AI-based integration), the bases of integration are remodeling the datasets and data collections \[[5](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_005)\].
    
    ### 13.6.2 Data scarcity and limited availability
    
    As mentioned previously, the basis of truthful AI-based integration is high-quality, valid, and comprehensive datasets, and these narratives are essential for training AI in order to get elevations in DDS and ML models. However, access to such data can be limited or restricted to preexisting narrow figures, particularly in rare disease conditions or new therapeutic areas that are still underdeveloped or require special considerations \[[63](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_063)\].
    
    Accurate predictions in developing delivery systems or remodeling existing designs using AI models majorly demand a significant amount of data so the best possible results can be obtained. In many situations or disease states, there may be limited data available for drug under use or population in which the condition prevails, this leads us to less accurate predictions with unclear progression or biased results which lack credibility \[[64](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_064)\].
    
    For instance, there are many rare diseases that may have limited data available, or they might have regional data with limited variations considered valid or accurate for targeting a larger population or people with different genetics, which can be a significant challenge in making the development of AI models less refined and resourceful. In addition to that, the data used to model and train AI systems may not be able to represent the population of interest or, even so, will not be able to consider special parameters that the population acquires, which can lead to biased discriminatory results lacking validity to be used for drug design development \[[65](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_065)\].
    
    In addition to that, some types of datasets, such as longitudinal data or real-world evidence, may not be easily available. All these parameters lead to the limited use of AI models. By keeping in mind all the mentioned shortcomings, it becomes crucial to develop careful data considerations that aim quality and evident representation of the data that is to be used to develop AI models \[[64](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_064)\].
    
    ### 13.6.3 Data privacy and security
    
    The ground for AI-integrated studies aims at using patient data, which is extremely sensitive and private to every patient and institution dealing with the condition; therefore, it is crucial to provide strict privacy protection policies and prevent data breaches at all costs. This involves complete compliance with data protection regulations (such as the General Data Protection Regulation). Due to strict privacy considerations, data collection and subsequent validation as per the rules and policies of privacy protection regulations become a challenge for AI model design and its further use in developmental studies \[[63](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_063)\].
    
    The use of data is aimed at providing decision-making models that demand a huge dataset to make accurate and better-informed decisions; hence, data privacy and security are major parameters in this. Therefore, it means that data collected from clients or obtained by requesting patients’ need to be shared and validated with the agencies and authorities running the drug development programs and legal measures of AI modeling. All these considerations make it necessary to safeguard and protect the client’s or patient’s information in the whole process. This results in developing public trust in AI-driven drug development, which leads to transparency of the system and information about the AI system will be utilized, its current and possible benefits, and its limitations \[[66](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_066)\].
    
    In order to ensure high morality and sensibility in AI integration design, it is necessary to address these challenges. When handling sensitive patient or special cases, their privacy and integrity must be kept intact so that the data can be effectively used for AI-driven decision-making. This gives patients confidence that their data and information are kept secure and are only used for the betterment of existing complications, for their own good and social benefit. So better encryption and safety give evident trust in regulating the datasets and literature this involves the creation of policies for the usage of data and regulations related to consent. Moreover, patients should be given full access to their data and provided insight into how the data is being used \[[67](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_067)\].
    
    ### 13.6.4 Transparency and regulatory obstacles
    
    The use of AI models leads us to understand the use of complex algorithms that serve as the backbone of AI integration within DDS. These algorithms are known as “black boxes” The reason to call them black boxes is that it is quite complicated to develop an understanding of how the model arrives at its predictions and anticipates possibilities. Because of the lack of transparency, this becomes an obstacle in acquiring public trust and a challenge in gaining regulatory approval from related authorities to use AI-based drug development tools. This is mainly due to the difficulty in demonstrating how the model provides accurate and reliable predictions with authentic results.
    
    Further issues with the lack of transparency lead to limited trust in the model’s predictions and analyzing tools. This becomes more evident if the model’s prediction is not satisfactory and conflicts with the theoretical research conducted by clinicians and drug development researchers, with the prediction failing to accurately pinpoint the outcome \[[64](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_064)\].
    
    AI models demand training, and for this validation, AI algorithms require enormous, high-quality, well-defined datasets. Such data is not easily available, or even if it is, the quantity is scarce, making it challenging to obtain. These are the considerations one must think about, particularly when acquiring data from medical professionals, academics, and data scientists to guarantee authentic and trustworthy data. Additionally, from the perspective of patient privacy, data-sharing agreements should be developed with full attention to detail \[[67](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_067)\].
    
    ### 13.6.5 Drug delivery hurdles and model drift
    
    Over time, AI predictive models face a variety of challenges in the development of DDS. Among these challenges, one to consider is the requirement for accurately designed predictive models that offer regulated drug discharge. This is because, over the course of time, the data used to develop the predictive model becomes outdated, mainly due to changes in clinical practices or treatment protocols. Hence, this phenomenon is called model drift. For AI integration to work accurately, the predictive model should be kept updated, and regular retraining of the model becomes necessary. This can become resource-draining and a challenge for specialists to implement.
    
    In using AI, we overcome this issue by utilizing nanocarriers and primarily developing nano systems that are aided and stimulated via artificial intelligence. For example, the penetration of drugs in the ocular tissue of the eyes is generally limited, the reason being the physiological and anatomical barriers within the eye leading to reduced penetration of any foreign matter. So the AI predictive models keep this physiology in consideration and use nanotechnology like nano micelles, nanoparticles, and liposomes, to give accurate delivery keeping in mind the ocular barriers \[[65](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_065)\].
    
    To identify and develop newer therapeutic targets and agents, as well as to enhance delivery systems to revolutionize currently available therapeutics, a detailed and thoughtful collaboration between AI researchers and pharmaceutical experts is extremely necessary. The problem arises in collaboration because of differences in learning attitudes and methodology in available knowledge, information, educational culture, and internal communication. This can be overcome by using user-friendly consumer interfaces that will promote clinicians in using AI collaboration \[[67](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_067)\]
    
    ### 13.6.6 Ethical considerations in AI applications in biomedical fields
    
    AI integrations demand data, so the use of data, its privacy, biases equity, and accessibility are always questioned, which demands AI to utilize given datasets morally and sensibly, specifically when dealing with patient-sensitive data \[[67](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_067)\].
    
    ### 13.6.7 Data privacy and security
    
    Data privacy is an essential consideration in ethical parameters, as biomedical AI systems demand a huge dataset and a vast quantity of sensitive health data; hence, this causes a potential risk of data breaches. Patient health data are essential for AI to make wise decisions; therefore, the protection of this data is crucial for patient privacy. There are certain regulations and laws explained by the general data protection regulation (GDPR) that are mainly implemented in the European Union, and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) implemented in the United States \[[67](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_067)\].
    
    ### 13.6.8 Fairness and bias
    
    Training data are firstly needed by AI systems to generate AI algorithms; hence, if the training datasets do not represent a special population or underserved communities, developing a biased pickup of data resulting in discrimination against a particular socioeconomic status. To prevent this, regular audits must be run and measured to ensure mitigation should be implemented \[[67](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_067)\].
    
    ### 13.6.9 Explainability and transparency
    
    AI systems operate on algorithms that are not completely understood; hence, they are termed as black boxes. They lack interpretability, leading to a lack of explainability regarding why and to whom the result of an AI prediction could be implemented. This also leads to patient concerns. Due to these parameters, it becomes difficult to distinguish and choose between AI predictive models and the more understandable traditional models of drug designing \[[68](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_068)\].
    
    ### 13.6.10 Accountability and liability
    
    Like any model, AI is also a software-run model of predictions; hence, it can also provide false information or incomplete results. It is necessary to develop a legal regulation that targets who to hold accountable if the AI model fails to give desired results or gives false data. This is a dual-use concerned matter where both the AI developer as well as the person at the consumer end should be accountable for errors \[[68](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_068)\].
    
    ## 13.7 Limitations of predictive modeling and virtual screening
    
    ### 13.7.1 Data quality and reliability
    
    When we are using AI predictive models, the basic focus is on high-quality data. In case the training data is biased, the model will not give accurate results, especially if newer material or a rare disease state is being studied. This leads to researchers and material scientists making inaccurate predictions and limiting their trust in computing infrastructure. To overcome this, we need to opt for advanced optimization technology and modify robust models \[[69](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_069)\].
    
    ### 13.7.2 Experimental validation and model accuracy
    
    AI models and virtual screening need to be validated by experimental analysis, although this requires extensive testing and costly handling that can be time-consuming. Yet, this offers great predictability regarding how efficiently a model works under given conditions or real-world challenges. Additionally, when provided with newer datasets or a complex real-world setting, the accuracy of an AI model might vary from its training dataset. Hence, careful consideration related to data modeling must be undertaken. For example, when dealing with in silico models, virtual screening has to be validated with experimental analysis that leads to slow discovery \[[69](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_069)\].
    
    ### 13.7.3 Limited applicability and need for assistance
    
    When designing or discovering a newer material the researchers should consider that a predictive model might work only effectively within the dataset used as their training data; hence, it becomes necessary to adjust their research methodology following these tools \[[69](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_069)\].
    
    ### 13.7.4 Performance misestimation and biological complications
    
    In AI predictive models, the performance of a system is often judged using benchmarks (meaning how existing datasets influence the model’s performance). In AI-integrated ML or VS, we first need to introduce a training set of data, and then a comparative study is conducted to estimate how well the model works. In the case of biological testing, things get a little complicated, as the dynamic system of biological system makes it difficult for ML and predictive models to give a very accurate result. However, modern AI predictive models use special considerations in this regard for excellent results \[[70](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_070)\].
    
    ## 13.8 Future directions
    
    The rapid progression in ML and the convergence of AI in drug discovery and development have proven to be fruitful in all fields of medicine, whether it’s the advancement of novel drugs, AI-driven polymer designs, multi-use polymers,, or the potential use of personalized medication. All these advancements are now possible with the aid of AI integration and ML \[[71](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_071)\].
    
    ### 13.8.1 Emerging trends in AI and smart polymer research
    
    #### 13.8.1.1 Drug discovery and virtual testing
    
    AI predictive modeling is being highly effective in target identification and development of DDS, either by HTS  or virtual screening \[[65](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_065)\]. The accurate predictability and larger dataset availability make it possible for researchers to use AI-integrated virtual clinical trials, which result in cutting costs and reducing time-consuming data generation; hence, the success rates and the correct way to conduct the study design are predicted \[[71](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_071)\].
    
    #### 13.8.1.2 AI-driven drug delivery systems
    
    AI integration in the development of DDS that respond to parameters studied and embedded into ML models helps design drugs with special triggers for release \[[72](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_072)\]. Moreover, AI-driven nanotechnology is revolutionizing drug carrier systems, offering accurate and effective drug delivery with limited off-target effects and precise dosing. Smart pills are also a new concept introduced by AI \[[71](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_071)\].
    
    #### 13.8.1.3 Autonomous experimentation a new progress
    
    A new concept in the development of DDS is the active learning by ML agents, in which datasets are generated specially for materials that are expensive to produce or their measure parameters are tedious. One of the most common approaches among them is Bayesian optimization. All these utilize active learning algorithms, hence requiring no intervention from a researcher \[[72](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_072)\].
    
    Their major advantage is that they help in discovering desired materials and polymers using HTS or ML, which require no time to rest. Among the new progression is the use of reversible addition–fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT); it helps in finding the most desired polymer characteristic properties, such as 19 F magnetic resonance signal (MRI) signal for contrast agents \[[72](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_072)\].
    
    #### 13.8.1.4 Potential for personalized medicine through AI-enhanced drug delivery systems
    
    The modern concept of personalized medication has revolutionized the traditional medication and healthcare system. This approach proves to be effective as it aims at using genetics in order to understand medical needs and to intervene them accordingly. This approach helps enhance patient outcomes and provides a smooth path for evolving precise healthcare and treatment \[[73](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_073)\].
    
    AI and ML prove to be an excellent helping hand in predicting pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of special genetics and target populations, aiding in the development of personalized therapeutics. By using predictive algorithms and analyzing patient datasets, AI predicts accurate treatment strategies with responses obtained via trial designs. This helps healthcare providers use accurate measures to diagnose and then treat conditions as per individual patient characteristics and biomarkers as helping tools. AI and ML have a huge potential in evolving the pharmaceutical industry with high accuracy drug designing and healthcare delivery systems \[[73](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_073)\].
    
    #### 13.8.1.5 Enhancing drug efficacy with AI
    
    Drug efficacy is a major reason why AI is remodeling and evolving personalized medicine. With up-to-date datasets and advanced algorithms, AI is able to analyze and optimize possible drug responses, helping to develop better treatment strategies that improve patient outcomes. This becomes more evident in chronic conditions, helping in development of treatment as per individual patient needs. By drawing comparisons, considering genetic factors, and evaluating drug effectiveness, a predictive model can estimate the right drug in the right dosage form, for the right period of time, in the right amount, and for the right patient. AI enhancement in personalized medication is very fruitful in chemotherapy as it prevents trial-and-error-based issues. Chronic conditions like diabetes and hypertension can also be better treated using AI modeling \[[73](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_073)\].
    
    #### 13.8.1.6 Collaborative approaches between AI researchers and material scientists
    
    A cooperation and collaboration between AI and material scientists help in improving discovery and development, providing breakthrough advancements in both fields.
    
    #### 13.8.1.7 Material discovery and experimental investigations
    
    New material discovery faces a major challenge of experimental analysis that aims at predicting properties. However, the use of AI integration helps fasten up the process, providing effective and efficient experimentation \[[74](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_074)\].
    
    #### 13.8.1.8 Material optimization
    
    AI-driven models can predict material characteristics more accurately and also optimize them using physical modeling at atomic or macromolecular levels. This can be done using past data or the generation of new datasets that enable faster predictions and help organize and obtain data and literature from the tremendous datasets and databases available through AI models \[[74](#chapter-013.xhtml#b_9783111681870-013_ref_074)\].
    
    ## 13.9 Conclusion
    
    Over the past few years, DDS have gone through significant advancements. Smart polymer drug delivery designs proved to be of great effectivity making them excellent drug carriers and considered for further innovations. AI proved its part in the pharmaceutical field by advancing DDS and integrating smart polymers through AI-driven predictive modeling, ML, deep learning, and VSTs. The advanced characterization of nanomaterials, enhanced by AI that involves image processing, toxicology assessment, and rheological studies, have given complete insight for advanced drug delivery and polymer designing.
    
    Despite having many advantages, AI integrations also face some challenges that mainly revolve around the availability of quality, precise, and reliable data that is unbiased following all the ethical standards.
    
    The future innovations in drug discovery, efficacy, and personalized medication are all integrated by modern AI models. AI integration will lead material scientists to develop optimal polymer designs, paving brighter pathways for efficient DDS.
